Good! Speak to the mariners: fall to't yarely, or / we run ourselves aground: bestir, bestir.
Good! Talk to the sailors. Get to work quickly, or we'll run aground. Move, move!
Heigh, my hearts! cheerly, cheerly, my hearts! / yare, yare! Take in the topsail. Tend to th' master's / whistle.—Blow till thou burst thy wind, if room enough.
Come on, my lads! Cheer up, cheer up, my lads! Quick, quick! Take in the topsail. Listen for the captain's whistle. Blow till you burst, wind, as long as we have room to move.
Good boatswain, have care. Where's the master? / Play the men.
Good boatswain, be careful. Where's the captain? Make the men work like men.
Do you not hear him? You mar our labour: / keep your cabins: you do assist the storm.
Can't you hear him? You're getting in the way of our work. Stay in your cabins: you're helping the storm.
When the sea is. Hence! What cares these / roarers for the name of king? To cabin! silence! Trouble / us not.
I will when the sea is. Get away! What do these roaring waves care about the title of king? To your cabins! Quiet! Don't bother us.
Good, yet remember whom thou hast aboard.
All right, but remember who you have on board.

None that I more love than myself. You are counsellor: if you can / command these elements to silence, and work the peace of the present, / we will not hand a rope more. Use your authority: if you cannot, give / thanks you have lived so long, and make yourself ready in your cabin / for the mischance of the hour, if it so hap.—Cheerly, good / hearts!—Out of our way, I say.

Nobody I love more than myself. You're a royal adviser: if you can order these elements to be quiet and make peace right now, we won't touch another rope. Use your authority. If you can't, be thankful you've lived so long, and go to your cabin and get ready for disaster, if it comes to that. Cheer up, lads! Out of our way, I said.

I have great comfort from this fellow. Methinks / he hath no drowning mark upon him: his complexion is / perfect gallows. Stand fast, good Fate, to his hanging! / make the rope of his destiny our cable, for our own doth / little advantage! If he be not born to be hang'd, our / case is miserable.

This fellow is a great comfort to me. I don't think he's marked for drowning: he has the look of a man born to be hanged. Hold to it, good Fate, and hang him! Let the rope of his destiny be our anchor cable, since ours does us little good! If he wasn't born to be hanged, we're in a bad way.
Down with the topmast! yare! lower, lower! / Bring her to try wi' th' maincourse. [A cry within] A / plague upon this howling! They are louder than the / weather or our office.—
Down with the topmast! Quick! Lower, lower! Try to hold her steady with the mainsail. A curse on this howling! They're louder than the storm or our shouting orders.
Yet again! What do you here? Shall we give o'er, and / drown? Have you a mind to sink?
Here again! What are you doing here? Should we give up and drown? Do you want to sink?
A pox o' your throat, you bawling, blasphemous, / incharitable dog!
A plague on your throat, you yelling, swearing, heartless dog!
Hang, cur, hang! you whoreson, insolent noisemaker, / we are less afraid to be drowned than thou art.
Hang, you mongrel, hang! You son of a whore, you rude loudmouth, we're less afraid of drowning than you are.
I'll warrant him for drowning, though the ship were / no stronger than a nutshell, and as leaky as an unstanched / wench.
I promise he won't drown, even if the ship were no stronger than a nutshell and as leaky as a loose woman.
Lay her a-hold, a-hold! set her two courses: off / to sea again: lay her off.
Hold her into the wind! Set the two mainsails! Back out to sea! Steer her away from shore!
All lost! to prayers, to prayers! all lost!
All is lost! Pray, pray! All is lost!
What, must our mouths be cold?
The King and Prince at prayers! let us assist them, / For our case is as theirs.
The King and the Prince are praying! Let's join them, because we're in the same danger.
We are merely cheated of our lives by drunkards.— / This wide-chapp'd rascal—would thou might'st lie drowning / The washing of ten tides!
We're simply being cheated out of our lives by drunkards. This big-mouthed rascal: I wish you'd lie drowning while ten tides washed over you!
He'll be hang'd yet, / Though every drop of water swear against it, / And gape at wid'st to glut him.
He'll be hanged yet, even if every drop of water swears he won't and opens wide to swallow him.
Let's all sink wi' the King.
Let's all go down with the King.
Now would I give a thousand furlongs of sea for / an acre of barren ground; long heath, brown furze, any / thing. The wills above be done! but I would fain die / dry death.
Right now I'd give a thousand miles of sea for an acre of barren land: long heather, brown gorse, anything. Heaven's will be done! But I'd rather die a dry death.

If by your art, my dearest father, you have / Put the wild waters in this roar, allay them. / The sky, it seems, would pour down stinking pitch, / But that the sea, mounting to th' welkin's cheek, / Dashes the fire out. O! I have suffered / With those that I saw suffer: a brave vessel, / Who had, no doubt, some noble creatures in her, / Dash'd all to pieces. O! the cry did knock / Against my very heart. Poor souls, they perish'd. / Had I been any god of power, I would / Have sunk the sea within the earth, or e'er / It should the good ship so have swallow'd and / The fraughting souls within her.

If your magic, my dearest father, has made the wild waters roar like this, calm them. It looks as if the sky would pour down stinking tar, except that the sea, rising up to the face of the heavens, puts out its fire. Oh, I have suffered with those I saw suffering! A fine ship, which surely had some noble people in it, smashed to pieces. Oh, their cry hit my very heart! Poor souls, they died. If I had been a powerful god, I would have sunk the sea into the earth before it could swallow the good ship like that, with all the souls it carried.
Be collected: / No more amazement: tell your piteous heart / There's no harm done.
Calm yourself. No more alarm. Tell your pitying heart that no harm has been done.

No harm. / I have done nothing but in care of thee, / Of thee, my dear one, thee, my daughter, who / Art ignorant of what thou art, nought knowing / Of whence I am: nor that I am more better / Than Prospero, master of a full poor cell, / And thy no greater father.

No harm. Everything I have done has been to take care of you, you, my dear one, my daughter, who doesn't know who you are, and knows nothing of where I come from, or that I am far greater than Prospero, the master of a very poor cave, and your father, nothing more.
More to know / Did never meddle with my thoughts.
It never crossed my mind to want to know more.
'Tis time / I should inform thee farther. Lend thy hand, / And pluck my magic garment from me.—So:
It's time I told you more. Give me your hand and help me take off my magic cloak. There.

Lie there my art.—Wipe thou thine eyes; have comfort. / The direful spectacle of the wrack, which touch'd / The very virtue of compassion in thee, / I have with such provision in mine art / So safely ordered that there is no soul— / No, not so much perdition as an hair / Betid to any creature in the vessel / Which thou heard'st cry, which thou saw'st sink. Sit down; / For thou must now know farther.

Lie there, my magic. Dry your eyes and take heart. I have used my art so carefully to stage the dreadful sight of that shipwreck, which stirred all your compassion, that not one soul, not so much as a hair of anyone in that ship, which you heard cry out and saw sink, has been lost. Sit down, because now you must learn more.
You have often / Begun to tell me what I am: but stopp'd, / And left me to a bootless inquisition, / Concluding 'Stay; not yet.'
You've often started to tell me who I am, but stopped, and left me wondering in vain, ending with 'Wait; not yet.'

The hour's now come, / The very minute bids thee ope thine ear; / Obey, and be attentive. Canst thou remember / A time before we came unto this cell? / I do not think thou canst: for then thou wast not / Out three years old.

The time has come. This very minute tells you to open your ears. Do as I say and listen closely. Can you remember a time before we came to this cave? I don't think you can, because you weren't quite three years old then.
By what? By any other house, or person? / Of any thing the image, tell me, that / Hath kept with thy remembrance.
Remember what? Some other house, or person? Tell me any picture of anything that has stayed in your memory.
'Tis far off, / And rather like a dream than an assurance / That my remembrance warrants. Had I not / Four, or five, women once, that tended me?
It's a long way off, and more like a dream than something my memory can swear to. Didn't I once have four or five women who looked after me?

Thou hadst, and more, Miranda. But how is it / That this lives in thy mind? What seest thou else / In the dark backward and abysm of time? / If thou rememb'rest aught ere thou cam'st here, / How thou cam'st here, thou mayst.

You did, and more, Miranda. But how is it that this stays in your mind? What else do you see in the dark distant past? If you remember anything from before you came here, you might remember how you came here.
Twelve year since, Miranda, twelve year since, / Thy father was the Duke of Milan, and / A prince of power.
Twelve years ago, Miranda, twelve years ago, your father was the Duke of Milan and a powerful prince.
Sir, are not you my father?
Thy mother was a piece of virtue, and / She said thou wast my daughter: and thy father / Was Duke of Milan, and his only heir / And princess,—no worse issued.
Your mother was a model of virtue, and she said you were my daughter. And your father was Duke of Milan, and his only heir was a princess, no less nobly born.
O, the heavens! / What foul play had we that we came from thence? / Or blessed was't we did?
Oh, heavens! What foul play forced us out of there? Or was it a blessing that we left?
Both, both, my girl. / By foul play, as thou say'st, were we heav'd thence; / But blessedly holp hither.
Both, both, my girl. We were thrown out by foul play, as you say, but helped here by a blessing.
O! my heart bleeds / To think o' th' teen that I have turn'd you to, / Which is from my remembrance. Please you, further.
Oh, my heart bleeds to think of the grief I must have caused you, which I can't remember. Please go on.

My brother and thy uncle, call'd Antonio— / I pray thee, mark me,—that a brother should / Be so perfidious!—he, whom next thyself, / Of all the world I lov'd, and to him put / The manage of my state; as at that time / Through all the signories it was the first, / And Prospero the prime duke, being so reputed / In dignity, and for the liberal arts, / Without a parallel: those being all my study, / The government I cast upon my brother, / And to my state grew stranger, being transported / And rapt in secret studies. Thy false uncle— / Dost thou attend me?

My brother, your uncle, called Antonio (please listen to me), that a brother could be so treacherous! He was the one I loved most in the world after you, and I gave him the running of my state. At that time Milan was the first of all the Italian states, and Prospero the leading duke, famous for his rank and without equal in learning. Since learning was all I cared about, I handed the government to my brother and grew a stranger to my own state, carried away and absorbed in secret studies. Your treacherous uncle... are you listening to me?

Being once perfected how to grant suits, / How to deny them, who t' advance, and who / To trash for over-topping; new created / The creatures that were mine, I say, or chang'd 'em, / Or else new form'd 'em: having both the key / Of officer and office, set all hearts i' th' state / To what tune pleas'd his ear: that now he was / The ivy which had hid my princely trunk, / And suck'd my verdure out on't.—Thou attend'st not.

Once he had mastered how to grant requests and how to refuse them, whom to promote and whom to cut down for growing too tall, he remade the officials who were loyal to me: he either replaced them or changed their loyalties. Holding the key both to the officers and to their posts, he tuned every heart in the state to whatever pleased his ear. So he became the ivy that hid my princely trunk and sucked the life out of it. You're not listening.

I pray thee, mark me. / I thus neglecting worldly ends, all dedicated / To closeness and the bettering of my mind / With that, which, but by being so retir'd, / O'er-priz'd all popular rate, in my false brother / Awak'd an evil nature; and my trust, / Like a good parent, did beget of him / A falsehood, in its contrary as great / As my trust was; which had indeed no limit, / A confidence sans bound. He being thus lorded, / Not only with what my revenue yielded, / But what my power might else exact,—like one / Who having, into truth, by telling of it, / Made such a sinner of his memory, / To credit his own lie,—he did believe / He was indeed the Duke; out o' the substitution, / And executing th' outward face of royalty, / With all prerogative.—Hence his ambition growing— / Dost thou hear?

Please listen to me. I neglected worldly matters and gave myself to solitude and the improvement of my mind, with studies that, if they hadn't kept me so withdrawn, would have been worth more than anything the people value. This woke an evil nature in my treacherous brother. My trust, like a good parent with a bad child, produced in him a falseness as great as my trust, which truly had no limit, a confidence without bounds. Made a lord in this way, not only with my income but with whatever else my power could demand, he was like a man who tells a lie so often that he cheats his own memory into believing it. He came to believe that he really was the Duke, because he was standing in for me and acting out the outward show of royalty with all its privileges. So his ambition grew. Do you hear me?
Your tale, sir, would cure deafness.
Your story, sir, would cure deafness.

To have no screen between this part he play'd / And him he play'd it for, he needs will be / Absolute Milan. Me, poor man—my library / Was dukedom large enough: of temporal royalties / He thinks me now incapable; confederates,— / So dry he was for sway,—wi' th' King of Naples / To give him annual tribute, do him homage; / Subject his coronet to his crown, and bend / The dukedom, yet unbow'd—alas, poor Milan!— / To most ignoble stooping.

To remove any barrier between the part he played and the man he played it for, he was determined to be Duke of Milan outright. As for me, poor man, my library was dukedom enough: he now thinks me unfit to rule. He was so thirsty for power that he made a deal with the King of Naples to pay him yearly tribute and do him homage, to place his duke's coronet under the King's crown, and to bend the dukedom, which had never bowed (alas, poor Milan!), into shameful submission.
Mark his condition, and the event; then tell me / If this might be a brother.
Note the terms of his deal and what happened, then tell me if this could be a brother.
I should sin / To think but nobly of my grandmother: / Good wombs have borne bad sons.
It would be a sin to think anything but well of my grandmother. Good mothers have given birth to bad sons.

Now the condition. / This King of Naples, being an enemy / To me inveterate, hearkens my brother's suit; / Which was, that he, in lieu o' the premises / Of homage and I know not how much tribute, / Should presently extirpate me and mine / Out of the dukedom, and confer fair Milan, / With all the honours on my brother: whereon, / A treacherous army levied, one midnight / Fated to the purpose, did Antonio open / The gates of Milan; and, i' th' dead of darkness, / The ministers for th' purpose hurried thence / Me and thy crying self.

Now hear the terms. This King of Naples, a long-standing enemy of mine, listened to my brother's request. It was that, in return for homage and who knows how much tribute, the King should immediately throw me and my family out of the dukedom and give fair Milan, with all its honours, to my brother. So a treacherous army was raised, and one midnight, chosen for the purpose, Antonio opened the gates of Milan, and in the dead of darkness his agents hurried me and you, crying, out of the city.
Alack, for pity! / I, not rememb'ring how I cried out then, / Will cry it o'er again: it is a hint / That wrings mine eyes to't.
Oh, how sad! I don't remember how I cried then, but I'll cry over it again. The story wrings tears from my eyes.
Hear a little further, / And then I'll bring thee to the present business / Which now's upon us; without the which this story / Were most impertinent.
Hear a little more, and then I'll bring you to the business we're dealing with now, without which this story would be pointless.
Wherefore did they not / That hour destroy us?
Why didn't they kill us there and then?

Well demanded, wench: / My tale provokes that question. Dear, they durst not, / So dear the love my people bore me, nor set / A mark so bloody on the business; but / With colours fairer painted their foul ends. / In few, they hurried us aboard a bark, / Bore us some leagues to sea, where they prepared / A rotten carcass of a boat, not rigg'd, / Nor tackle, sail, nor mast: the very rats / Instinctively have quit it. There they hoist us, / To cry to th' sea, that roar'd to us: to sigh / To th' winds, whose pity, sighing back again, / Did us but loving wrong.

A good question, girl: my story invites it. My dear, they didn't dare, because my people loved me so much, and they didn't want to leave such a bloody stain on their business. Instead they painted over their foul aims with fairer colours. In short, they hurried us onto a ship and carried us some miles out to sea, where they had got ready a rotten wreck of a boat, with no rigging, ropes, sail or mast: even the rats had instinctively left it. There they put us, to cry to the sea, which roared back at us, and to sigh to the winds, whose pity, sighing back, only did us loving harm.
Alack! what trouble / Was I then to you!
Oh, what a burden I must have been to you then!

O, a cherubin / Thou wast that did preserve me! Thou didst smile, / Infused with a fortitude from heaven, / When I have deck'd the sea with drops full salt, / Under my burden groan'd: which rais'd in me / An undergoing stomach, to bear up / Against what should ensue.

Oh, you were a little angel who saved me! You smiled, filled with a courage from heaven, while I wept salt tears into the sea and groaned under my burden. Your smile gave me the courage to endure whatever was coming.

By Providence divine. / Some food we had and some fresh water that / A noble Neapolitan, Gonzalo, / Out of his charity,—who being then appointed / Master of this design,—did give us, with / Rich garments, linens, stuffs, and necessaries, / Which since have steaded much: so, of his gentleness, / Knowing I lov'd my books, he furnish'd me, / From mine own library with volumes that / I prize above my dukedom.

By God's providence. We had some food and some fresh water, which a noble man of Naples, Gonzalo, out of kindness, gave us, since he had been put in charge of the plan. He also gave us rich clothes, linen, cloth and other necessities, which have been very useful since. And in the same kindness, knowing I loved my books, he gave me volumes from my own library that I value more than my dukedom.
Would I might / But ever see that man!
I wish I could see that man some day!

Sit still, and hear the last of our sea-sorrow. / Here in this island we arriv'd: and here / Have I, thy schoolmaster, made thee more profit / Than other princes can, that have more time / For vainer hours, and tutors not so careful.

Sit still and hear the end of our sea story. We arrived on this island, and here I, as your teacher, have given you a better education than other princesses get, who have more time for idle pastimes and tutors who are less careful.
Heavens thank you for't! And now, I pray you, sir,— / For still 'tis beating in my mind,—your reason / For raising this sea-storm?
Heaven thank you for it! And now, please, sir, since it is still pounding in my mind, why did you raise this storm?

Know thus far forth. / By accident most strange, bountiful Fortune, / Now my dear lady, hath mine enemies / Brought to this shore; and by my prescience / I find my zenith doth depend upon / A most auspicious star, whose influence / If now I court not but omit, my fortunes / Will ever after droop. Here cease more questions; / Thou art inclin'd to sleep; 'tis a good dulness, / And give it way;—I know thou canst not choose.—

Know this much. By a very strange accident, generous Fortune, now my friend, has brought my enemies to this shore. And I can see by my foreknowledge that my highest point depends on a very lucky star: if I don't seize its influence now but let it pass, my fortunes will sink for ever after. No more questions now. You're drowsy. It's a good sleepiness, so give in to it. I know you can't help it.
Come away, servant, come! I am ready now. / Approach, my Ariel; Come!
Come here, servant, come! I'm ready now. Come close, my Ariel. Come!

All hail, great master! grave sir, hail! I come / To answer thy best pleasure; be't to fly, / To swim, to dive into the fire, to ride / On the curl'd clouds; to thy strong bidding task / Ariel and all his quality.

Greetings, great master! Wise sir, greetings! I've come to do whatever you wish, whether it's to fly, to swim, to dive into fire, or to ride on the curling clouds. Set Ariel and all his fellow spirits to work on your strong command.
Hast thou, spirit, / Perform'd to point the tempest that I bade thee?
Spirit, did you perform the storm exactly as I told you?

To every article. / I boarded the King's ship; now on the beak, / Now in the waist, the deck, in every cabin, / I flam'd amazement; sometime I'd divide, / And burn in many places; on the topmast, / The yards, and boresprit, would I flame distinctly, / Then meet and join: Jove's lightning, the precursors / O' th' dreadful thunder-claps, more momentary / And sight-outrunning were not: the fire and cracks / Of sulphurous roaring the most mighty Neptune / Seem to besiege and make his bold waves tremble, / Yea, his dread trident shake.

Down to every detail. I boarded the King's ship. Now at the bow, now in the middle, on the deck, in every cabin, I blazed up terror. Sometimes I split myself and burned in many places at once; on the topmast, the yards and the bowsprit I would flame separately, then meet and join together. Jove's lightning bolts, which come before the terrible thunderclaps, were not quicker or more dazzling. The fire and the cracks of sulphur-smelling roaring seemed to lay siege to mighty Neptune himself, make his bold waves tremble, and even shake his dreadful trident.
My brave spirit! / Who was so firm, so constant, that this coil / Would not infect his reason?
My brave spirit! Was anyone so steady and calm that this uproar didn't affect his mind?

Not a soul / But felt a fever of the mad, and play'd / Some tricks of desperation. All but mariners / Plunged in the foaming brine and quit the vessel, / Then all afire with me: the King's son, Ferdinand, / With hair up-staring—then like reeds, not hair— / Was the first man that leapt; cried 'Hell is empty, / And all the devils are here.'

Not a soul. Every one of them felt a madman's fever and did something desperate. All except the sailors plunged into the foaming sea and abandoned the ship, which was all on fire with me. The King's son, Ferdinand, with his hair standing on end like reeds, not hair, was the first man to jump. He cried, 'Hell is empty, and all the devils are here.'
Why, that's my spirit! / But was not this nigh shore?
That's my spirit! But wasn't this close to shore?

Not a hair perish'd; / On their sustaining garments not a blemish, / But fresher than before: and, as thou bad'st me, / In troops I have dispers'd them 'bout the isle. / The king's son have I landed by himself, / Whom I left cooling of the air with sighs / In an odd angle of the isle, and sitting, / His arms in this sad knot.

Not a hair was lost. Their clothes, which kept them afloat, don't have a stain on them; they're fresher than before. And as you told me, I've scattered them in groups around the island. The King's son I brought ashore by himself. I left him cooling the air with his sighs in a remote corner of the island, sitting with his arms folded sadly, like this.
Of the King's ship / The mariners, say how thou hast dispos'd, / And all the rest o' th' fleet?
Tell me what you've done with the sailors of the King's ship, and all the rest of the fleet.

Safely in harbour / Is the King's ship; in the deep nook, where once / Thou call'dst me up at midnight to fetch dew / From the still-vex'd Bermoothes; there she's hid: / The mariners all under hatches stowed; / Who, with a charm join'd to their suff'red labour, / I have left asleep: and for the rest o' th' fleet / Which I dispers'd, they all have met again, / And are upon the Mediterranean flote / Bound sadly home for Naples, / Supposing that they saw the king's ship wrack'd, / And his great person perish.

The King's ship is safe in harbour, in the deep bay where you once called me up at midnight to fetch dew from the always stormy Bermudas. She's hidden there. The sailors are all stowed below deck; with a spell added to their exhaustion I have left them asleep. As for the rest of the fleet, which I scattered, they have all met up again and are on the Mediterranean sea, sailing sadly home to Naples, believing they saw the King's ship wrecked and the King himself die.
Ariel, thy charge / Exactly is perform'd; but there's more work: / What is the time o' th' day?
Ariel, you have done your job exactly, but there is more work to do. What time of day is it?
At least two glasses. The time 'twixt six and now / Must by us both be spent most preciously.
By at least two hours. The time between now and six o'clock must be used very carefully by both of us.
Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, / Let me remember thee what thou hast promis'd, / Which is not yet perform'd me.
Is there more work? Since you're giving me more labour, let me remind you of what you promised me, which you haven't given me yet.
How now! moody? / What is't thou canst demand?
What's this? Sulking? What can you possibly ask for?
Before the time be out! No more!
Before your time is up? Not another word!
I prithee, / Remember I have done thee worthy service; / Told thee no lies, made no mistakings, serv'd / Without or grudge or grumblings: thou didst promise / To bate me a full year.
Please remember that I have served you well. I've told you no lies, made no mistakes, and served you without any resentment or complaining. You promised to cut a whole year off my service.
Dost thou forget / From what a torment I did free thee?
Have you forgotten the torment I freed you from?
Thou dost; and think'st it much to tread the ooze / Of the salt deep, / To run upon the sharp wind of the north, / To do me business in the veins o' th' earth / When it is bak'd with frost.
You have. And you think it's a lot to walk on the mud of the salty sea bed, to run on the sharp north wind, to do my work in the veins of the earth when it's frozen hard.
Thou liest, malignant thing! Hast thou forgot / The foul witch Sycorax, who with age and envy / Was grown into a hoop? Hast thou forgot her?
You're lying, you spiteful thing! Have you forgotten the foul witch Sycorax, who was bent double with age and malice? Have you forgotten her?
Thou hast. Where was she born? / Speak; tell me.
You have. Where was she born? Speak, tell me.

O! was she so? I must / Once in a month recount what thou hast been, / Which thou forget'st. This damn'd witch Sycorax, / For mischiefs manifold, and sorceries terrible / To enter human hearing, from Argier, / Thou know'st, was banish'd: for one thing she did / They would not take her life. Is not this true?

Oh, was she? Once a month I have to remind you what you've been, since you forget it. This damned witch Sycorax, as you know, was banished from Algiers for countless crimes and for sorceries too terrible for human ears. Because of one thing she did, they wouldn't execute her. Isn't that true?

This blue-ey'd hag was hither brought with child, / And here was left by the sailors. Thou, my slave, / As thou report'st thyself, wast then her servant: / And, for thou wast a spirit too delicate / To act her earthy and abhorr'd commands, / Refusing her grand hests, she did confine thee, / By help of her more potent ministers, / And in her most unmitigable rage, / Into a cloven pine; within which rift / Imprison'd, thou didst painfully remain / A dozen years; within which space she died, / And left thee there, where thou didst vent thy groans / As fast as mill-wheels strike. Then was this island— / Save for the son that she did litter here, / A freckl'd whelp, hag-born—not honour'd with / A human shape.

This hag with the blue-ringed eyes was brought here pregnant and left here by the sailors. You, my slave, as you describe yourself, were her servant then. And because you were a spirit too delicate to carry out her coarse and hateful orders, and refused her great commands, she imprisoned you, with the help of her stronger servants and in her most relentless rage, in a split pine tree. Imprisoned in that crack you stayed in pain for twelve years. During that time she died and left you there, where you groaned as fast as the paddles of a mill wheel strike the water. At that time this island had no human form to honour it, except for the son she gave birth to here, a freckled pup born of a hag.

Dull thing, I say so; he, that Caliban, / Whom now I keep in service. Thou best know'st / What torment I did find thee in; thy groans / Did make wolves howl, and penetrate the breasts / Of ever-angry bears: it was a torment / To lay upon the damn'd, which Sycorax / Could not again undo; it was mine art, / When I arriv'd and heard thee, that made gape / The pine, and let thee out.

That's what I said, stupid: that Caliban whom I now keep as a servant. You know best what torment I found you in. Your groans made wolves howl and pierced the hearts of ever-angry bears. It was a torment fit for the damned, which Sycorax could not undo. It was my magic, when I arrived and heard you, that made the pine split open and let you out.
If thou more murmur'st, I will rend an oak / And peg thee in his knotty entrails till / Thou hast howl'd away twelve winters.
If you complain any more, I'll split an oak and peg you inside its knotty insides until you've howled away twelve winters.
Pardon, master: / I will be correspondent to command, / And do my spriting gently.
Forgive me, master. I'll obey your commands and do my spirit work willingly.
Do so; and after two days / I will discharge thee.
Do that, and in two days I'll set you free.
That's my noble master! / What shall I do? Say what? What shall I do?
That's my noble master! What shall I do? Tell me what? What shall I do?
Go make thyself like a nymph o' th' sea: be subject / To no sight but thine and mine; invisible / To every eyeball else. Go, take this shape, / And hither come in 't: go, hence with diligence!
Go and turn yourself into a sea nymph. Be visible to no eyes but yours and mine, invisible to everyone else's. Go, take this shape and come back here in it. Go now, and hurry!
Awake, dear heart, awake! thou hast slept well; / Awake!
Wake up, dear heart, wake up! You've slept well. Wake up!
[Waking] The strangeness of your story put / Heaviness in me.
The strangeness of your story made me drowsy.
Shake it off. Come on; / We'll visit Caliban my slave, who never / Yields us kind answer.
Shake it off. Come on, we'll visit my slave Caliban, who never gives us a kind answer.
'Tis a villain, sir, / I do not love to look on.
He's a villain, sir, and I don't like looking at him.
But as 'tis, / We cannot miss him: he does make our fire, / Fetch in our wood; and serves in offices / That profit us.—What ho! slave! Caliban! / Thou earth, thou! Speak.
But as things are, we can't do without him. He makes our fire, fetches our wood, and does jobs that are useful to us. Hey there! Slave! Caliban! You lump of earth! Speak.
Come forth, I say; there's other business for thee: / Come, thou tortoise! when?
Come out, I said. There's other work for you. Come on, you tortoise! When are you coming?
Fine apparition! My quaint Ariel, / Hark in thine ear.
A fine sight! My clever Ariel, listen closely.
My lord, it shall be done.
My lord, it will be done.
Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself / Upon thy wicked dam, come forth!
You poisonous slave, fathered by the devil himself on your wicked mother, come out!
As wicked dew as e'er my mother brush'd / With raven's feather from unwholesome fen / Drop on you both! A south-west blow on ye, / And blister you all o'er!
May dew as poisonous as any my mother ever swept with a raven's feather from an unhealthy swamp drop on both of you! May a south-west wind blow on you and cover you in blisters!

For this, be sure, to-night thou shalt have cramps, / Side-stitches that shall pen thy breath up; urchins / Shall forth at vast of night that they may work / All exercise on thee: thou shalt be pinch'd / As thick as honeycomb, each pinch more stinging / Than bees that made them.

For that, you can be sure, tonight you'll have cramps and stitches in your side that will choke your breath. Goblins in the shape of hedgehogs will come out in the dead of night to work all their torments on you. You'll be pinched as full of holes as a honeycomb, each pinch stinging more than the bees that made it.

I must eat my dinner. / This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, / Which thou tak'st from me. When thou cam'st first, / Thou strok'st me and made much of me; wouldst give me / Water with berries in't; and teach me how / To name the bigger light, and how the less, / That burn by day and night: and then I lov'd thee, / And show'd thee all the qualities o' th' isle, / The fresh springs, brine-pits, barren place, and fertile. / Curs'd be I that did so! All the charms / Of Sycorax, toads, beetles, bats, light on you! / For I am all the subjects that you have, / Which first was mine own king; and here you sty me / In this hard rock, whiles you do keep from me / The rest o' th' island.

I have to eat my dinner. This island is mine, through my mother Sycorax, and you're taking it from me. When you first came, you stroked me and made a fuss of me. You gave me water with berries in it, and taught me the names of the bigger light and the smaller one that burn by day and night. And then I loved you, and showed you all the features of the island: the fresh springs, the salt pits, the barren places and the fertile ones. Curse me for doing it! May all the spells of Sycorax, toads, beetles, bats, fall on you! I am the only subject you have, and I used to be my own king. Now you pen me like a pig in this hard rock, while you keep the rest of the island from me.

Thou most lying slave, / Whom stripes may move, not kindness! I have us'd thee, / Filth as thou art, with human care, and lodg'd thee / In mine own cell, till thou didst seek to violate / The honour of my child.
You lying slave, who can be moved by whipping but not by kindness! Filth as you are, I treated you with human care and let you live in my own cave, until you tried to rape my child.
Oh ho! Oh ho! Would it had been done! / Thou didst prevent me; I had peopl'd else / This isle with Calibans.
Oh ho! Oh ho! I wish I had done it! You stopped me, or else I would have filled this island with little Calibans.

Abhorred slave, / Which any print of goodness wilt not take, / Being capable of all ill! I pitied thee, / Took pains to make thee speak, taught thee each hour / One thing or other: when thou didst not, savage, / Know thine own meaning, but wouldst gabble like / A thing most brutish, I endow'd thy purposes / With words that made them known: but thy vile race, / Though thou didst learn, had that in't which good natures / Could not abide to be with; therefore wast thou / Deservedly confin'd into this rock, who hadst / Deserv'd more than a prison.

Hateful slave, who will take no mark of goodness and is capable of every evil! I pitied you. I took pains to teach you to speak, taught you one thing or another every hour. When you, savage, didn't know your own meaning but would gabble like a brute, I gave your thoughts words to make them known. But your vile nature, though you learned, had something in it that good natures could not bear to be near. So you were rightly confined to this rock, though you deserved more than a prison.
You taught me language, and my profit on't / Is, I know how to curse: the red plague rid you, / For learning me your language!
You taught me language, and all I've gained from it is that I know how to curse. May the red plague kill you for teaching me your language!

Hag-seed, hence! / Fetch us in fuel; and be quick, thou 'rt best, / To answer other business. Shrug'st thou, malice? / If thou neglect'st, or dost unwillingly / What I command, I'll rack thee with old cramps, / Fill all thy bones with aches; make thee roar, / That beasts shall tremble at thy din.

Child of a hag, go! Fetch us firewood, and you'd better be quick, so you can do other jobs. Are you shrugging, you spiteful thing? If you neglect or do unwillingly what I command, I'll torture you with old people's cramps, fill all your bones with aches, and make you roar so loud that wild animals will tremble at your noise.
No, pray thee.— / [Aside] I must obey. His art is of such power, / It would control my dam's god, Setebos, / And make a vassal of him.
No, please! I have to obey. His magic is so powerful it could control my mother's god, Setebos, and make him his servant.

Come unto these yellow sands, / And then take hands: / Curtsied when you have, and kiss'd,— / The wild waves whist,— / Foot it featly here and there; / And, sweet sprites, the burden bear. / Hark, hark! / [Burden: Bow, wow, dispersedly.] / The watch dogs bark: / [Burden: Bow, wow, dispersedly.] / Hark, hark! I hear / The strain of strutting Chanticleer / [Cry, Cock-a-diddle-dow.]

Come to these yellow sands, and then join hands. When you have bowed and kissed, and the wild waves are hushed, dance nimbly here and there, and, sweet spirits, sing the chorus. Listen, listen! The watchdogs bark. Listen, listen! I hear the call of the strutting rooster.

Where should this music be? i' th' air or th' earth? / It sounds no more;—and sure it waits upon / Some god o' th' island. Sitting on a bank, / Weeping again the king my father's wrack, / This music crept by me upon the waters, / Allaying both their fury and my passion, / With its sweet air: thence I have follow'd it,— / Or it hath drawn me rather,—but 'tis gone. / No, it begins again.

Where can this music be coming from? The air or the earth? It has stopped. Surely it is playing for some god of the island. While I sat on a bank, weeping again over the wreck of my father the King, this music crept past me over the waters, calming both their fury and my grief with its sweet tune. I have followed it from there, or rather it has drawn me, but it's gone. No, it's starting again.

Full fathom five thy father lies: / Of his bones are coral made: / Those are pearls that were his eyes: / Nothing of him that doth fade / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange. / Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell: / [Burden: Ding-dong.] / Hark! now I hear them—ding-dong, bell.

Your father lies thirty feet deep. His bones have turned to coral, and those are pearls that were his eyes. Nothing of him that might decay but has been changed by the sea into something rich and strange. Sea nymphs ring his funeral bell every hour. Listen! Now I hear them: ding-dong, bell.
The ditty does remember my drown'd father. / This is no mortal business, nor no sound / That the earth owes:—I hear it now above me.
The song remembers my drowned father. This is no human doing, and no sound that belongs to the earth. Now I hear it above me.
The fringed curtains of thine eye advance, / And say what thou seest yond.
Lift up the fringed curtains of your eyes and tell me what you see over there.
What is't? a spirit? / Lord, how it looks about! Believe me, sir, / It carries a brave form:—but 'tis a spirit.
What is it? A spirit? Lord, how it looks around! Believe me, sir, it has a splendid shape. But it's a spirit.

No, wench; it eats and sleeps, and hath such senses / As we have, such; this gallant which thou see'st / Was in the wrack; and but he's something stain'd / With grief,—that beauty's canker,—thou mightst call him / A goodly person: he hath lost his fellows / And strays about to find 'em.

No, girl. It eats and sleeps and has the same senses we have, the very same. This fine young man you see was in the shipwreck. If he weren't somewhat marked by grief, which eats away at beauty, you might call him handsome. He has lost his companions and is wandering about looking for them.
I might call him / A thing divine; for nothing natural / I ever saw so noble.
I would call him something divine, because I've never seen anything natural so noble.
[Aside] It goes on, I see, / As my soul prompts it.—Spirit, fine spirit! I'll free thee / Within two days for this.
It's going just as I planned. Spirit, fine spirit! I'll free you within two days for this.

Most sure, the goddess / On whom these airs attend!—Vouchsafe, my prayer / May know if you remain upon this island; / And that you will some good instruction give / How I may bear me here: my prime request, / Which I do last pronounce, is,—O you wonder!— / If you be maid or no?

Surely this is the goddess whom this music serves! Please grant my prayer and tell me if you live on this island, and give me some good advice on how to behave here. My chief request, which I make last, is (oh, you wonder!) whether you are a human girl or not?
No wonder, sir; / But certainly a maid.
No wonder, sir, but certainly a girl.
My language! Heavens!— / I am the best of them that speak this speech, / Were I but where 'tis spoken.
She speaks my language! Heavens! I would be the highest-ranking person who speaks it, if I were back where it's spoken.
How! the best? / What wert thou, if the King of Naples heard thee?
What? The highest? What would you be if the King of Naples heard you?

A single thing, as I am now, that wonders / To hear thee speak of Naples. He does hear me; / And, that he does, I weep: myself am Naples, / Who with mine eyes,—never since at ebb,—beheld / The King, my father wrack'd.

A lone man, as I am now, who is amazed to hear you speak of Naples. The King of Naples does hear me, and I weep because he does. I myself am King of Naples, since I saw with my own eyes, which have not stopped crying since, the King my father wrecked.
Yes, faith, and all his lords, the Duke of Milan, / And his brave son being twain.
Yes, truly, and all his lords, including the Duke of Milan and his fine son.

[Aside.] The Duke of Milan, / And his more braver daughter could control thee, / If now 'twere fit to do't.—At the first sight [Aside.] / They have changed eyes;—delicate Ariel, / I'll set thee free for this!—[To FERDINAND] A word, good sir: / I fear you have done yourself some wrong: a word.

The real Duke of Milan and his even finer daughter could prove you wrong, if this were the right time. At first sight they have fallen in love. Delicate Ariel, I'll set you free for this! A word, good sir. I'm afraid you've made a mistake. A word.
[Aside.] Why speaks my father so ungently? This / Is the third man that e'er I saw; the first / That e'er I sigh'd for; pity move my father / To be inclin'd my way!
Why does my father speak so roughly? This is the third man I've ever seen, and the first I've ever sighed for. May pity move my father to feel as I do!
[Aside.] O! if a virgin, / And your affection not gone forth, I'll make you / The Queen of Naples.
Oh, if you're a virgin and you haven't given your heart to anyone, I'll make you Queen of Naples.

Soft, sir; one word more— / [Aside] They are both in either's powers: but this swift / business I must uneasy make, lest too light winning / Make the prize light. [To FERDINAND] One word more: / I charge thee / That thou attend me. Thou dost here usurp / The name thou ow'st not; and hast put thyself / Upon this island as a spy, to win it / From me, the lord on't.

Wait, sir, one more word. They're both in each other's power. But I must make this quick business difficult, in case winning too easily makes the prize seem cheap. One more word. I order you to listen to me. You are claiming a title that isn't yours, and you've come to this island as a spy, to take it from me, its lord.
No, as I am a man.
No, on my word as a man.
There's nothing ill can dwell in such a temple: / If the ill spirit have so fair a house, / Good things will strive to dwell with't.
Nothing evil can live in such a temple. If an evil spirit had such a beautiful house, good things would fight to live there with it.

[To FERDINAND] Follow me.— / [To MIRANDA] Speak not you for him; he's a traitor.— / [To FERDINAND] Come; / I'll manacle thy neck and feet together: / Sea-water shalt thou drink; thy food shall be / The fresh-brook mussels, wither'd roots, and husks / Wherein the acorn cradled. Follow.

Follow me. Don't speak up for him: he's a traitor. Come on. I'll chain your neck and feet together. You'll drink sea water, and your food will be freshwater mussels, withered roots and the husks that held acorns. Follow me.
No; / I will resist such entertainment till / Mine enemy has more power.
No. I'll resist that kind of treatment until my enemy proves stronger than me.
O dear father! / Make not too rash a trial of him, for / He's gentle, and not fearful.
Oh, dear father, don't judge him too harshly and too quickly. He's noble, not a coward.

What! I say, / My foot my tutor? Put thy sword up, traitor; / Who mak'st a show, but dar'st not strike, thy conscience / Is so possess'd with guilt: come from thy ward, / For I can here disarm thee with this stick / And make thy weapon drop.

What? Is my foot going to teach me, its head? Put your sword away, traitor. You make a show of fighting but don't dare to strike, because your conscience is so full of guilt. Drop your guard, because I can disarm you with this stick and make your weapon fall.
Hence! Hang not on my garments.
Get away! Don't hang on my clothes.
Sir, have pity; / I'll be his surety.
Sir, have pity. I'll vouch for him.

Silence! One word more / Shall make me chide thee, if not hate thee. What! / An advocate for an impostor? hush! / Thou think'st there is no more such shapes as he, / Having seen but him and Caliban: foolish wench! / To the most of men this is a Caliban, / And they to him are angels.

Quiet! One more word will make me scold you, if not hate you. What! Speaking up for a fraud? Hush! You think there are no other men as handsome as him, having seen only him and Caliban. Foolish girl! Compared with most men, this one is a Caliban, and they are angels next to him.
My affections / Are then most humble; I have no ambition / To see a goodlier man.
Then my love is very humble. I have no wish to see a better-looking man.
[To FERDINAND] Come on; obey: / Thy nerves are in their infancy again, / And have no vigour in them.
Come on, obey. Your muscles are as weak as a baby's again and have no strength in them.

So they are: / My spirits, as in a dream, are all bound up. / My father's loss, the weakness which I feel, / The wrack of all my friends, nor this man's threats, / To whom I am subdued, are but light to me, / Might I but through my prison once a day / Behold this maid: all corners else o' th' earth / Let liberty make use of; space enough / Have I in such a prison.

So they are. My spirits are all tied up, as if in a dream. My father's loss, the weakness I feel, the wreck of all my friends, and the threats of this man who has overpowered me are all light burdens, if only I may see this girl through my prison window once a day. Let free men use every other corner of the earth: I'll have space enough in such a prison.
[Aside] It works.—[To FERDINAND] Come on.— / Thou hast done well, fine Ariel! [To FERDINAND] Follow me.— / [To ARIEL] Hark what thou else shalt do me.
It's working. Come on. You've done well, fine Ariel! Follow me. Listen to what else you must do for me.
Be of comfort; / My father's of a better nature, sir, / Than he appears by speech: this is unwonted, / Which now came from him.
Take heart. My father has a kinder nature, sir, than his words suggest. What he just said is not like him.
Thou shalt be as free / As mountain winds; but then exactly do / All points of my command.
You'll be as free as the mountain winds. But first, carry out every detail of my orders exactly.
[To FERDINAND] Come, follow.—Speak not for him.
Come, follow me. Don't speak up for him.

Beseech you, sir, be merry; you have cause, / So have we all, of joy; for our escape / Is much beyond our loss. Our hint of woe / Is common: every day, some sailor's wife, / The masters of some merchant and the merchant, / Have just our theme of woe; but for the miracle, / I mean our preservation, few in millions / Can speak like us: then wisely, good sir, weigh / Our sorrow with our comfort.

Please, sir, cheer up. You have reason to be joyful, as we all do, because our escape is far greater than our loss. Our cause for sorrow is common. Every day some sailor's wife, the officers of some merchant ship and the merchant himself have the same reason to grieve as we do. But as for the miracle, I mean our survival, very few in millions can talk like us. So, good sir, weigh our sorrow wisely against our comfort.
He receives comfort like cold porridge.
He takes comfort like cold porridge.
The visitor will not give him o'er so.
The comforter won't give up on him so easily.
Look, he's winding up the watch of his wit; by / and by it will strike.
Look, he's winding up the clock of his wit. Soon it will strike.
When every grief is entertain'd that's offer'd, / Comes to the entertainer—
When a man takes in every grief that comes his way, what he gets for it is...
Dolour comes to him, indeed: you have spoken / truer than you purposed.
Dolour, sorrow, is what he gets, indeed. You spoke more truly than you meant to.
You have taken it wiselier than I meant you should.
You took it more cleverly than I intended.
Fie, what a spendthrift is he of his tongue!
Ugh, how he wastes his tongue!
Well, I have done: but yet—
Which, of he or Adrian, for a good wager, first / begins to crow?
I'll bet you: who'll start crowing first, him or Adrian?
Though this island seem to be desert,—
Although this island seems to be deserted...
Ha, ha, ha! So, you're paid.
Ha, ha, ha! There, you've been paid.
Uninhabitable, and almost impossible to reach...
It must needs be of subtle, tender, and delicate / temperance.
It must have a fine, gentle and delicate climate.
Ay, and a subtle; as he most learnedly delivered.
Yes, and a fine one, as he so learnedly told us.
The air breathes upon us here most sweetly.
The air breathes on us very sweetly here.
As if it had lungs, and rotten ones.
As if it had lungs, and rotten ones.
Or, as 'twere perfum'd by a fen.
Or as if it had been perfumed by a swamp.
Here is everything advantageous to life.
Everything here is good for life.
True, except the means to live.
Of that there's none, or little.
There's none of that, or very little.
How lush and lusty the grass looks! how green!
How rich and healthy the grass looks! How green!
With an eye of green in't.
With a spot of green in it.
No; he doth but mistake the truth totally.
No, he just gets the truth completely wrong.
But the rarity of it is,—which is indeed almost / beyond credit,—
But the remarkable thing, which is almost beyond belief...
Like a lot of guaranteed marvels.
That our garments, being, as they were, drenched / in the sea, hold notwithstanding their freshness and / glosses, being rather new-dyed than stain'd with salt / water.
Is that our clothes, drenched in the sea as they were, have still kept their freshness and shine, as if they were newly dyed rather than stained with salt water.
If but one of his pockets could speak, would it / not say he lies?
If just one of his pockets could talk, wouldn't it say he's lying?
Ay, or very falsely pocket up his report.
Yes, or else very dishonestly hide what it knows.
Methinks, our garments are now as fresh as when / we put them on first in Afric, at the marriage of the / king's fair daughter Claribel to the King of Tunis.
I think our clothes are as fresh now as when we first put them on in Africa, at the marriage of the King's beautiful daughter Claribel to the King of Tunis.
'Twas a sweet marriage, and we prosper well in our return.
It was a lovely wedding, and we're doing very nicely on the way home.
Tunis was never graced before with such a paragon / to their queen.
Tunis was never honoured with such a perfect queen before.
Not since the time of the widow Dido.
Widow! a pox o' that! How came that widow in? Widow Dido!
Widow? Damn that! Where did that widow come from? Widow Dido!
What if he had said, widower Aeneas too? / Good Lord, how you take it!
What if he'd said 'widower Aeneas' as well? Good Lord, how you take things!
Widow Dido said you? You make me study of that; she was of / Carthage, not of Tunis.
Did you say widow Dido? You make me think about that. She was from Carthage, not Tunis.
His word is more than the miraculous harp.
His word is more powerful than the magic harp that built the walls of Thebes.
He hath rais'd the wall, and houses too.
He has raised the walls, and the houses too.
What impossible matter will he make easy next?
What impossible thing will he make easy next?
I think he will carry this island home in his / pocket, and give it his son for an apple.
I think he'll carry this island home in his pocket and give it to his son as an apple.
And, sowing the kernels of it in the sea, bring / forth more islands.
And plant its seeds in the sea to grow more islands.
[To ALONSO.] Sir, we were talking that our garments seem now / as fresh as when we were at Tunis at the marriage of / your daughter, who is now Queen.
Sir, we were saying that our clothes seem as fresh now as when we were in Tunis at the marriage of your daughter, who is now Queen.
And the rarest that e'er came there.
And the finest queen that ever came there.
Bate, I beseech you, widow Dido.
Except, if you please, widow Dido.
O! widow Dido; ay, widow Dido.
Oh, widow Dido! Yes, widow Dido.
Is not, sir, my doublet as fresh as the first day I / wore it? I mean, in a sort.
Isn't my jacket as fresh, sir, as on the first day I wore it? I mean, in a way.
That sort was well fish'd for.
He fished hard for that 'in a way'.
When I wore it at your daughter's marriage?
When I wore it at your daughter's marriage?

You cram these words into mine ears against / The stomach of my sense. Would I had never / Married my daughter there! for, coming thence, / My son is lost; and, in my rate, she too, / Who is so far from Italy remov'd, / I ne'er again shall see her. O thou, mine heir / Of Naples and of Milan! what strange fish / Hath made his meal on thee?

You stuff these words into my ears though my mind has no appetite for them. I wish I had never married my daughter off there! Because on the way back from there my son was lost, and, as I see it, she is lost too, since she is so far from Italy that I'll never see her again. Oh, my heir to Naples and Milan, what strange fish has made a meal of you?

Sir, he may live: / I saw him beat the surges under him, / And ride upon their backs: he trod the water, / Whose enmity he flung aside, and breasted / The surge most swoln that met him: his bold head / 'Bove the contentious waves he kept, and oar'd / Himself with his good arms in lusty stroke / To th' shore, that o'er his wave-worn basis bowed, / As stooping to relieve him. I not doubt / He came alive to land.

Sir, he may be alive. I saw him beat the waves beneath him and ride on their backs. He trod the water, pushing aside its hostility, and met the most swollen wave head on. He kept his bold head above the battling waves and rowed himself with strong strokes of his good arms to the shore, whose cliff, worn away by waves, bent over as if stooping to help him. I'm sure he reached land alive.

Sir, you may thank yourself for this great loss, / That would not bless our Europe with your daughter, / But rather lose her to an African; / Where she, at least, is banish'd from your eye, / Who hath cause to wet the grief on't.

Sir, you have only yourself to thank for this great loss. You wouldn't bless Europe with your daughter but chose to lose her to an African. There she's at least banished from your sight, which has good reason to weep over it.

You were kneel'd to, and importun'd otherwise / By all of us; and the fair soul herself / Weigh'd between loathness and obedience at / Which end o' th' beam should bow. We have lost your son, / I fear, for ever: Milan and Naples have / More widows in them of this business' making, / Than we bring men to comfort them; the fault's your own.

All of us knelt to you and begged you not to do it. And the fair girl herself was torn between reluctance and obedience, unable to decide which way the scales should tip. We have lost your son, I fear, for ever. Milan and Naples have more widows because of this business than we are bringing men home to comfort them. The fault is your own.
So is the dearest of the loss.
So is the worst of the loss.
My lord Sebastian, / The truth you speak doth lack some gentleness / And time to speak it in; you rub the sore, / When you should bring the plaster.
My lord Sebastian, the truth you speak lacks kindness and a proper time to say it. You rub the sore when you should bring the bandage.
It is foul weather in us all, good sir, / When you are cloudy.
It's foul weather in all of us, good sir, when you are clouded over.
Had I plantation of this isle, my lord,—
If I had the colonising of this island, my lord...
He'd sow it with nettle seeds.
And were the king on't, what would I do?
And if I were king of it, what would I do?
'Scape being drunk for want of wine.
Avoid getting drunk, for lack of wine.

I' the commonwealth I would by contraries / Execute all things; for no kind of traffic / Would I admit; no name of magistrate; / Letters should not be known; riches, poverty, / And use of service, none; contract, succession, / Bourn, bound of land, tilth, vineyard, none; / No use of metal, corn, or wine, or oil; / No occupation; all men idle, all: / And women too, but innocent and pure; / No sovereignty,—

In my state I would do everything the opposite way from usual. I would allow no kind of trade, no title of magistrate. Reading and writing would be unknown. There would be no riches, no poverty and no servants. No contracts, no inheritance, no boundaries or fences, no ploughed fields or vineyards. No use of metal, grain, wine or oil. No jobs: all men idle, all of them, and women too, but innocent and pure. No ruler...
Yet he would be king on't.
And yet he'd be king of it.
The latter end of his commonwealth forgets the beginning.
The end of his state forgets its beginning.

All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavour; treason, felony, / Sword, pike, knife, gun, or need of any engine, / Would I not have; but nature should bring forth, / Of it own kind, all foison, all abundance, / To feed my innocent people.

Nature would produce everything for everyone in common, without sweat or effort. Treason, crime, swords, spears, knives, guns or any need for weapons I would not have. Instead nature would bring forth, by itself, every kind of plenty and abundance to feed my innocent people.
None, man: all idle; whores and knaves.
None, man. All idle: whores and scoundrels.
I would with such perfection govern, sir, / To excel the golden age.
I would govern so perfectly, sir, that I'd surpass the golden age.
And... are you listening to me, sir?
Prithee, no more: thou dost talk nothing to me.
Please, no more. What you say means nothing to me.
I do well believe your highness; and did it to / minister occasion to these gentlemen, who are of such / sensible and nimble lungs that they always use to laugh / at nothing.
I quite believe your Highness. I said it to give these gentlemen a chance, since their lungs are so sensitive and quick that they always laugh at nothing.
It was you we laughed at.
Who in this kind of merry fooling am nothing to / you; so you may continue, and laugh at nothing still.
And in this kind of merry fooling I am nothing compared with you. So you may carry on and laugh at nothing still.
What a blow was there given!
An it had not fallen flat-long.
If only it hadn't landed with the flat of the blade.
You are gentlemen of brave mettle: you would / lift the moon out of her sphere, if she would continue / in it five weeks without changing.
You are gentlemen of fine spirit. You would lift the moon out of her orbit if she stayed in it for five weeks without changing.
We would so, and then go a-bat-fowling.
We would, and then use her as a lamp to go hunting birds at night.
Nay, good my lord, be not angry.
No, my good lord, don't be angry.
No, I warrant you; I will not adventure my / discretion so weakly. Will you laugh me asleep, for I am / very heavy?
No, I promise you, I won't risk my good judgment on something so trivial. Will you laugh me to sleep? I feel very drowsy.
Go to sleep and listen to us.
What! all so soon asleep! I wish mine eyes / Would, with themselves, shut up my thoughts: I find / They are inclin'd to do so.
What! All asleep so soon! I wish my eyes would close and shut off my thoughts as well. I feel they want to.
Please you, sir, / Do not omit the heavy offer of it: / It seldom visits sorrow; when it doth, / It is a comforter.
Please, sir, don't refuse the drowsiness that's being offered. It seldom comes to people in sorrow, and when it does, it brings comfort.
We two, my lord, / Will guard your person while you take your rest, / And watch your safety.
We two, my lord, will guard you while you rest and watch over your safety.
What a strange drowsiness possesses them!
What a strange drowsiness has come over them!
It is the quality o' th' climate.
It's the effect of the climate.
Why / Doth it not then our eyelids sink? I find not / Myself dispos'd to sleep.
Then why doesn't it make our eyelids droop? I don't feel at all sleepy.

Nor I: my spirits are nimble. / They fell together all, as by consent; / They dropp'd, as by a thunder-stroke. What might, / Worthy Sebastian? O! what might?—No more:— / And yet methinks I see it in thy face, / What thou should'st be: The occasion speaks thee; and / My strong imagination sees a crown / Dropping upon thy head.

Nor do I. My mind is wide awake. They all fell asleep together, as if by agreement; they dropped as if struck by lightning. What might happen, worthy Sebastian? Oh, what might? No more. And yet I think I see in your face what you ought to be. The opportunity calls to you, and my strong imagination sees a crown dropping onto your head.
Do you not hear me speak?

I do: and surely / It is a sleepy language, and thou speak'st / Out of thy sleep. What is it thou didst say? / This is a strange repose, to be asleep / With eyes wide open; standing, speaking, moving, / And yet so fast asleep.

I can, and surely it's the language of sleep, and you're talking in your sleep. What was it you said? This is a strange kind of rest, to be asleep with your eyes wide open, standing, speaking, moving, and yet fast asleep.
Noble Sebastian, / Thou let'st thy fortune sleep—die rather: wink'st / Whiles thou art waking.
Noble Sebastian, you let your good fortune sleep, or rather die. You keep your eyes shut while you're awake.
Thou dost snore distinctly: / There's meaning in thy snores.
You snore clearly. There's meaning in your snores.
I am more serious than my custom; you / Must be so too, if heed me: which to do / Trebles thee o'er.
I'm more serious than usual. You must be serious too, if you listen to me, and doing that will make you three times greater.
I'll teach you how to flow.
I'll teach you how to flow in.
Do so: to ebb, / Hereditary sloth instructs me.
Do that. My natural laziness, born a younger brother, teaches me to ebb.

O! / If you but knew how you the purpose cherish / Whiles thus you mock it! how, in stripping it, / You more invest it! Ebbing men indeed, / Most often, do so near the bottom run / By their own fear or sloth.
Oh, if only you knew how much you love the idea while you mock it! How, by making light of it, you show how much you want it! Men on the ebb usually run aground because of their own fear or laziness.
Prithee, say on: / The setting of thine eye and cheek proclaim / A matter from thee, and a birth, indeed / Which throes thee much to yield.
Please, go on. The look in your eye and your face show you have something to say, something it pains you to bring out.

Thus, sir: / Although this lord of weak remembrance, this / Who shall be of as little memory / When he is earth'd, hath here almost persuaded,— / For he's a spirit of persuasion, only / Professes to persuade,—the King his son's alive, / 'Tis as impossible that he's undrown'd / As he that sleeps here swims.

It's this, sir. This lord with a weak memory, who will be just as little remembered once he's buried, has almost persuaded the King that his son is alive, since persuading is all he's good for. But it's as impossible that the son hasn't drowned as that this man sleeping here can swim.
I have no hope / That he's undrown'd.
I have no hope that he hasn't drowned.

O! out of that 'no hope' / What great hope have you! No hope that way is / Another way so high a hope, that even / Ambition cannot pierce a wink beyond, / But doubts discovery there. Will you grant with me / That Ferdinand is drown'd?

Oh, what great hope you have in that 'no hope'! No hope in that direction is, in another direction, a hope so high that even ambition can't see any further and doubts what it sees there. Do you agree with me that Ferdinand is drowned?
Then tell me, / Who's the next heir of Naples?
Then tell me, who's the next heir to Naples?

She that is Queen of Tunis; she that dwells / Ten leagues beyond man's life; she that from Naples / Can have no note, unless the sun were post— / The Man i' th' Moon's too slow—till newborn chins / Be rough and razorable: she that from whom / We all were sea-swallow'd, though some cast again, / And by that destiny, to perform an act / Whereof what's past is prologue, what to come / In yours and my discharge.

The one who is Queen of Tunis; who lives thirty miles beyond the end of the world; who can get no news from Naples, unless the sun carried the post (the Man in the Moon is too slow), until newborn babies have beards to shave. The one we were all sailing back from when the sea swallowed us, though some of us were thrown up again, and destined by that to perform an act. What has happened is only the prologue; what comes next is up to you and me.
What stuff is this!—How say you? / 'Tis true, my brother's daughter's Queen of Tunis; / So is she heir of Naples; 'twixt which regions / There is some space.
What nonsense is this? What are you saying? It's true my brother's daughter is Queen of Tunis, and she is heir to Naples, and there is some distance between the two.

A space whose every cubit / Seems to cry out 'How shall that Claribel / Measure us back to Naples?—Keep in Tunis, / And let Sebastian wake.'—Say this were death / That now hath seiz'd them; why, they were no worse / Than now they are. There be that can rule Naples / As well as he that sleeps; lords that can prate / As amply and unnecessarily / As this Gonzalo: I myself could make / A chough of as deep chat. O, that you bore / The mind that I do! What a sleep were this / For your advancement! Do you understand me?

A distance where every foot seems to cry out, 'How will that Claribel follow us back to Naples? Stay in Tunis, and let Sebastian wake up.' Suppose this were death that has taken them now: they would be no worse off than they are. There are people who could rule Naples as well as the man sleeping here, and lords who could chatter as long and as pointlessly as this Gonzalo. I could teach a crow to talk as deeply. Oh, if only you thought as I do! What a sleep this would be for your advancement! Do you understand me?
And how does your content / Tender your own good fortune?
And how does your happiness welcome your own good luck?
I remember / You did supplant your brother Prospero.
I remember you overthrew your brother Prospero.
True. / And look how well my garments sit upon me; / Much feater than before; my brother's servants / Were then my fellows; now they are my men.
True. And look how well my clothes suit me, much better than before. My brother's servants used to be my equals; now they work for me.

Ay, sir; where lies that? If 'twere a kibe, / 'Twould put me to my slipper: but I feel not / This deity in my bosom: twenty consciences / That stand 'twixt me and Milan, candied be they / And melt ere they molest! Here lies your brother, / No better than the earth he lies upon, / If he were that which now he's like, that's dead: / Whom I, with this obedient steel,—three inches of it,— / Can lay to bed for ever; whiles you, doing thus, / To the perpetual wink for aye might put / This ancient morsel, this Sir Prudence, who / Should not upbraid our course. For all the rest, / They'll take suggestion as a cat laps milk: / They'll tell the clock to any business that / We say befits the hour.

Yes, sir, where is that? If it were a chilblain, it would make me wear a slipper. But I don't feel this god in my heart. If twenty consciences stood between me and Milan, they could turn to sugar and melt before they bothered me! Here lies your brother, no better than the earth he lies on, if he were what he now looks like, that is, dead. With this obedient blade, three inches of it, I can put him to bed for ever, while you, doing the same, could close the eyes for good of this old leftover, this Sir Caution, so he can't condemn what we do. As for the rest, they'll take a hint as easily as a cat laps milk. They'll say the time is right for any business we tell them suits the hour.

Thy case, dear friend, / Shall be my precedent: as thou got'st Milan, / I'll come by Naples. Draw thy sword: one stroke / Shall free thee from the tribute which thou pay'st, / And I the king shall love thee.
Your example, dear friend, will be my guide. Just as you got Milan, I'll get Naples. Draw your sword. One stroke will free you from the tribute you pay, and I, the King, will love you.
Draw together: / And when I rear my hand, do you the like, / To fall it on Gonzalo.
Draw together, and when I raise my hand, you do the same, to bring it down on Gonzalo.

My master through his art foresees the danger / That you, his friend, are in; and sends me forth— / For else his project dies—to keep thee living. / [Sings in GONZALO'S ear] / While you here do snoring lie, / Open-ey'd Conspiracy / His time doth take. / If of life you keep a care, / Shake off slumber, and beware. / Awake! awake!

My master knows by his magic the danger that you, his friend, are in, and sends me to keep you alive, or else his plan will fail. While you lie here snoring, wide-eyed conspiracy is seizing its chance. If you care about your life, shake off sleep and beware. Wake up! Wake up!
Then let us both be sudden.
Now, good angels / Preserve the King!
Now, good angels, protect the King!
Why, how now! Ho, awake! Why are you drawn? / Wherefore this ghastly looking?
What's going on? Hey, wake up! Why are your swords drawn? Why do you look so pale?
Whiles we stood here securing your repose, / Even now, we heard a hollow burst of bellowing / Like bulls, or rather lions; did't not wake you? / It struck mine ear most terribly.
While we stood here guarding your rest, just now we heard a hollow burst of bellowing, like bulls, or rather lions. Didn't it wake you? It struck my ears terribly.
O! 'twas a din to fright a monster's ear, / To make an earthquake: sure it was the roar / Of a whole herd of lions.
Oh, it was a noise to frighten a monster's ears, to cause an earthquake! Surely it was the roar of a whole pack of lions.

Upon mine honour, sir, I heard a humming, / And that a strange one too, which did awake me. / I shak'd you, sir, and cried; as mine eyes open'd, / I saw their weapons drawn:—there was a noise, / That's verily. 'Tis best we stand upon our guard, / Or that we quit this place: let's draw our weapons.

On my honour, sir, I heard a humming, and a strange one too, which woke me. I shook you, sir, and shouted. As my eyes opened I saw their weapons drawn. There was a noise, that's true. We'd better stay on guard, or leave this place. Let's draw our weapons.
Lead off this ground: and let's make further search / For my poor son.
Lead us away from here, and let's search further for my poor son.
Heavens keep him from these beasts! / For he is, sure, i' th' island.
Heaven keep him safe from these beasts! For surely he's on the island.
Prospero my lord shall know what I have done: / So, King, go safely on to seek thy son.
My lord Prospero will know what I have done. So, King, go safely on and look for your son.

All the infections that the sun sucks up / From bogs, fens, flats, on Prosper fall, and make him / By inch-meal a disease! His spirits hear me, / And yet I needs must curse. But they'll nor pinch, / Fright me with urchin-shows, pitch me i' the mire, / Nor lead me, like a firebrand, in the dark / Out of my way, unless he bid 'em; but / For every trifle are they set upon me: / Sometime like apes that mow and chatter at me, / And after bite me; then like hedge-hogs which / Lie tumbling in my bare-foot way, and mount / Their pricks at my foot-fall; sometime am I / All wound with adders, who with cloven tongues / Do hiss me into madness.—

May all the diseases the sun sucks up from bogs, swamps and marshes fall on Prospero and make him sick inch by inch! His spirits can hear me, and yet I have to curse. But they won't pinch me, scare me with goblins, throw me in the mud, or lead me off my path in the dark like a will-o'-the-wisp, unless he tells them to. But they're set on me for every little thing. Sometimes they're like apes that pull faces and chatter at me and then bite me; then like hedgehogs that lie curled up in my barefoot path and stick their prickles up as I step. Sometimes I'm all wrapped in snakes, who hiss me mad with their forked tongues.
Lo, now, lo! / Here comes a spirit of his, and to torment me / For bringing wood in slowly. I'll fall flat; / Perchance he will not mind me.
Look, look! Here comes one of his spirits to torment me for bringing the wood in slowly. I'll lie flat. Maybe he won't notice me.

Here's neither bush nor shrub to bear off any weather at all, and / another storm brewing; I hear it sing i' th' wind; yond same black / cloud, yond huge one, looks like a foul bombard that would shed his / liquor. / If it should thunder as it did before, I know not where to hide my / head: yond same cloud cannot choose but fall by pailfuls.—What have / we here? a man or a fish? dead or alive? A fish: he smells like a / fish: a very ancient and fish-like smell; a kind of not of the newest / Poor-John. / A strange fish! Were I in England now,—as once I was, and had but / this fish painted, not a holiday fool there but would give a piece of / silver: there would this monster make a man; any strange beast there / makes a man. / When they will not give a doit to relieve a lame beggar, they will lay / out ten to see a dead Indian. Legg'd like a man, and his fins like / arms! Warm, o' my troth! I do now let loose my opinion: hold it no / longer; this is no fish, but an islander, that hath lately suffered by / thunderbolt. / [Thunder] Alas, the storm is come again! My best way is to creep under / his gaberdine; there is no other shelter hereabout: misery acquaints a / man with strange bed-fellows. I will here shroud till the dregs of the / storm be past.

There isn't a bush or shrub here to keep off any weather at all, and another storm is brewing: I can hear it singing in the wind. That black cloud over there, that huge one, looks like a filthy leather wine jug about to spill its drink. If it thunders like it did before, I don't know where to hide my head. That cloud is bound to pour down by the bucketful. What have we here? A man or a fish? Dead or alive? A fish: he smells like a fish, a very old, fishy smell, a sort of stale dried cod. A strange fish! If I were in England now, as I once was, and had a painting of this fish on a sign, every fool out on a holiday would pay a silver coin to see it. This monster would make a man's fortune there; any strange beast makes a man's fortune there. They won't give a penny to help a crippled beggar, but they'll pay ten to see a dead Indian. He has legs like a man, and his fins are like arms! Warm, I swear! Now I'll let my opinion go and hold it no longer: this is no fish but an islander who has recently been struck by a thunderbolt. Oh no, the storm has come again! My best plan is to crawl under his cloak; there's no other shelter around here. Misery introduces a man to strange bedfellows. I'll hide here till the last of the storm has passed.

I shall no more to sea, to sea, / Here shall I die a-shore:— / This is a very scurvy tune to sing at a man's funeral: / Well, here's my comfort. / [Drinks] / The master, the swabber, the boatswain, and I, / The gunner, and his mate, / Lov'd Mall, Meg, and Marian, and Margery, / But none of us car'd for Kate: / For she had a tongue with a tang, / Would cry to a sailor 'Go hang!' / She lov'd not the savour of tar nor of pitch, / Yet a tailor might scratch her wher-e'er she did itch. / Then to sea, boys, and let her go hang. / This is a scurvy tune too: but here's my comfort. / [Drinks]

I'll go to sea no more, no more; here I'll die ashore. This is a very lousy tune to sing at a man's funeral. Well, here's my comfort. The captain, the deck-hand, the boatswain and I, the gunner and his mate, loved Mall, Meg, Marian and Margery, but none of us cared for Kate. For she had a sharp tongue and would shout at a sailor, 'Go hang!' She didn't like the smell of tar or pitch, but a tailor could scratch her wherever she itched. So off to sea, boys, and let her go hang! This is a lousy tune too, but here's my comfort.

What's the matter? Have we devils here? Do you put tricks upon us with / savages and men of Ind? Ha! I have not 'scaped drowning, to be afeard / now of your four legs; for it hath been said, As proper a man as ever / went on four legs cannot make him give ground: and it shall be said so / again, while Stephano breathes at 's nostrils.

What's the matter? Do we have devils here? Are you playing tricks on us with savages and Indians? Ha! I haven't escaped drowning to be scared now of your four legs. As the saying goes, the finest man who ever walked on four legs can't make him give ground, and it will be said again as long as Stephano breathes through his nose.
The spirit is tormenting me! Oh!

This is some monster of the isle with four legs, who hath got, as I / take it, an ague. Where the devil should he learn our language?
