I will / give him some relief, if it be but for that; if I can recover him and / keep him tame and get to Naples with him, he's a present for any / emperor that ever trod on neat's-leather.

This is some monster of the island with four legs, who has caught a fever, I think. Where the devil did he learn our language? I'll give him some relief, if only for that. If I can cure him and tame him and get him to Naples, he'll be a present fit for any emperor who ever walked in leather shoes.
Do not torment me, prithee; I'll bring my wood / home faster.
Don't torment me, please! I'll bring my wood home faster.

He's in his fit now and does not talk after the / wisest. He shall taste of my bottle: if he have never / drunk wine afore, it will go near to remove his fit. If / I can recover him, and keep him tame, I will not take / too much for him: he shall pay for him that hath him, / and that soundly.

He's having his fit now and isn't talking very sensibly. He shall taste my bottle. If he's never drunk wine before, it will almost cure his fit. If I can cure him and tame him, no price will be too high for him. Whoever gets him will pay for him, and pay well.
Thou dost me yet but little hurt; thou wilt anon, / I know it by thy trembling: now Prosper works upon thee.
You're not hurting me much yet, but you will soon, I can tell by your trembling. Now Prospero is working on you.

Come on your ways: open your mouth; here is / that which will give language to you, cat. Open your / mouth: this will shake your shaking, I can tell you, and / that soundly [gives CALIBAN a drink]: you cannot tell who's your / friend: open your chaps again.

Come along now, open your mouth. Here's something that will make you talk, cat. Open your mouth. This will shake off your shaking, I can tell you, and properly. You can't tell who your friend is. Open your jaws again.
I should know that voice: it should be—but he is / drowned; and these are devils. O! defend me.
I should know that voice. It must be... but he's drowned, and these are devils. Oh, protect me!

Four legs and two voices; a most delicate monster! / His forward voice now is to speak well of his / friend; his backward voice is to utter foul speeches, and / to detract. If all the wine in my bottle will recover / him, I will help his ague. Come. Amen! I will pour some / in thy other mouth.

Four legs and two voices: a really fine monster! His front voice is for speaking well of his friend; his back voice is for saying foul things and slander. If all the wine in my bottle will cure him, I'll treat his fever. Come on. Amen! I'll pour some into your other mouth.
Doth thy other mouth call me? Mercy! mercy! / This is a devil, and no monster: I will leave him: I / have no long spoon.
Is your other mouth calling me? Mercy! Mercy! This is a devil, not a monster. I'll leave him: I don't have a long spoon to sup with the devil.
Stephano!—If thou beest Stephano, touch me, and / speak to me; for I am Trinculo:—be not afeared—thy good / friend Trinculo.
Stephano! If you're Stephano, touch me and speak to me, because I'm Trinculo. Don't be scared: your good friend Trinculo.

If thou beest Trinculo, come forth. I'll pull / thee by the lesser legs: if any be Trinculo's legs, these / are they. Thou art very Trinculo indeed! How cam'st thou / to be the siege of this moon-calf? Can he vent Trinculos?

If you're Trinculo, come out. I'll pull you out by the smaller legs. If any of these are Trinculo's legs, these are. You really are Trinculo! How did you come to be this moon-calf's droppings? Can he poop out Trinculos?

I took him to be kill'd with a thunderstroke. / But art thou not drown'd, Stephano? I hope now thou are / not drown'd. Is the storm overblown? I hid me under the / dead moon-calf's gaberdine for fear of the storm. And / art thou living, Stephano? O Stephano, two Neapolitans / 'scaped!

I thought he'd been killed by a thunderbolt. But aren't you drowned, Stephano? I hope now you're not drowned. Has the storm blown over? I hid under the dead moon-calf's cloak because I was afraid of the storm. And are you alive, Stephano? Oh, Stephano, two men of Naples escaped!
Prithee, do not turn me about: my stomach is not constant.
Please don't spin me round. My stomach is unsteady.
[Aside] These be fine things, an if they be not sprites. / That's a brave god, and bears celestial liquor; / I will kneel to him.
These are fine things, if they aren't spirits. That's a splendid god, and he carries heavenly drink. I'll kneel to him.

How didst thou 'scape? How cam'st thou hither? swear / by this bottle how thou cam'st hither—I escaped upon / a butt of sack, which the sailors heaved overboard, by / this bottle! which I made of the bark of a tree, with / mine own hands, since I was cast ashore.

How did you escape? How did you get here? Swear on this bottle how you got here. I escaped on a barrel of sherry that the sailors threw overboard, I swear by this bottle, which I made out of tree bark with my own hands after I was washed ashore.
I'll swear upon that bottle to be thy true / subject, for the liquor is not earthly.
I'll swear on that bottle to be your loyal subject, because that drink isn't from this earth.
Here: swear then how thou escapedst.
Here, swear how you escaped, then.
Swum ashore, man, like a duck: I can swim like / a duck, I'll be sworn.
Swam ashore, man, like a duck. I can swim like a duck, I swear.
[Passing the bottle] Here, kiss the book [gives / TRINCULO a drink]. Though thou canst swim like a / duck, thou art made like a goose.
Here, kiss the book. Even if you can swim like a duck, you're built like a goose.
O Stephano! hast any more of this?
Oh, Stephano, have you got any more of this?
The whole butt, man: my cellar is in a rock by / the seaside, where my wine is hid. How now, moon-calf! / How does thine ague?
The whole barrel, man. My cellar is in a rock by the sea, where my wine is hidden. Well, moon-calf! How's your fever?
Hast thou not dropped from heaven?
Out o' the moon, I do assure thee: I was the Man / in the Moon, when time was.
Out of the moon, I assure you. I was the Man in the Moon once upon a time.
I have seen thee in her, and I do adore thee, my / mistress showed me thee, and thy dog and thy bush.
I've seen you in her, and I worship you. My mistress showed you to me, and your dog and your bush.
Come, swear to that; kiss the book; I will / furnish it anon with new contents; swear.
Come on, swear to that. Kiss the book. I'll fill it up again soon. Swear.
By this good light, this is a very shallow / monster.—I afeard of him!—A very weak monster. / —The Man i' the Moon! A most poor credulous / monster!—Well drawn, monster, in good sooth!
By this good daylight, this is a very simple-minded monster. Me, afraid of him? A very feeble monster. The Man in the Moon! A very poor, gullible monster! That was a good swig, monster, honestly!
I'll show thee every fertile inch o' the island; / And I will kiss thy foot. I prithee, be my god.
I'll show you every fertile inch of the island, and I'll kiss your foot. Please, be my god.
By this light, a most perfidious and drunken / monster: when his god's asleep, he'll rob his bottle.
By this light, a most treacherous and drunken monster! When his god's asleep, he'll steal his bottle.
I'll kiss thy foot: I'll swear myself thy subject.
I'll kiss your foot. I'll swear to be your subject.
Come on, then; down, and swear.
Come on, then. Down, and swear.
I shall laugh myself to death at this puppy-headed / monster. A most scurvy monster! I could find in / my heart to beat him,—
I'll laugh myself to death at this puppy-faced monster. A very lousy monster! I could find it in my heart to beat him...
But that the poor monster's in drink: an / abominable monster!
...except that the poor monster is drunk. A disgusting monster!

I'll show thee the best springs; I'll pluck thee / berries; / I'll fish for thee, and get thee wood enough. / A plague upon the tyrant that I serve! / I'll bear him no more sticks, but follow thee, / Thou wondrous man.

I'll show you the best springs. I'll pick berries for you. I'll fish for you and get you plenty of wood. A plague on the tyrant I serve! I won't carry him any more sticks, but follow you, you wonderful man.
A most ridiculous monster, to make a wonder of / a poor drunkard!
A ridiculous monster, to make a marvel out of a poor drunk!

I prithee, let me bring thee where crabs grow; / And I with my long nails will dig thee pig-nuts; / Show thee a jay's nest, and instruct thee how / To snare the nimble marmozet; I'll bring thee / To clust'ring filberts, and sometimes I'll get thee / Young scamels from the rock. Wilt thou go with me?

Please, let me take you to where crab apples grow, and I'll dig up earth-nuts for you with my long nails. I'll show you a jay's nest and teach you how to trap the quick little monkey. I'll take you to clusters of hazelnuts, and sometimes I'll get you young seabirds from the rocks. Will you come with me?

I prithee now, lead the way without any more / talking—Trinculo, the king and all our company else / being drowned, we will inherit here.—Here, bear my / bottle.—Fellow Trinculo, we'll fill him by and by / again.

Now please lead the way without any more talking. Trinculo, since the King and all the rest of our company are drowned, we'll take over here. Here, carry my bottle. Fellow Trinculo, we'll fill it up again soon.
A howling monster, a drunken monster.
A howling monster, a drunken monster!

No more dams I'll make for fish; / Nor fetch in firing / At requiring, / Nor scrape trenchering, nor wash dish; / 'Ban 'Ban, Ca—Caliban, / Has a new master—Get a new man. / Freedom, high-day! high-day, freedom! freedom, / high-day, freedom!

I won't make dams for fish any more, or fetch firewood when I'm told, or scrape plates or wash dishes. 'Ban, 'Ban, Ca-Caliban has a new master: get a new servant! Freedom, hooray! Hooray, freedom! Freedom, hooray, freedom!
O brave monster! lead the way.
Oh, splendid monster! Lead the way.

There be some sports are painful, and their labour / Delight in them sets off: some kinds of baseness / Are nobly undergone, and most poor matters / Point to rich ends. This my mean task / Would be as heavy to me as odious; but / The mistress which I serve quickens what's dead, / And makes my labours pleasures: O! she is / Ten times more gentle than her father's crabbed, / And he's compos'd of harshness. I must remove / Some thousands of these logs, and pile them up, / Upon a sore injunction: my sweet mistress / Weeps when she sees me work, and says such baseness / Had never like executor. I forget: / But these sweet thoughts do even refresh my labours, / Most busy, least when I do it.

Some pastimes are hard work, but the pleasure in them makes up for the effort. Some kinds of lowly work can be done nobly, and many humble tasks lead to rich rewards. This menial job of mine would be as heavy as it is hateful to me, but the lady I serve brings dead things to life and turns my labours into pleasures. Oh, she is ten times kinder than her father is bad-tempered, and he is made of harshness. I have to move some thousands of these logs and pile them up, under a strict order. My sweet lady weeps when she sees me work and says such lowly work never had such a noble worker. I'm forgetting my job, but these sweet thoughts refresh my labours, and I'm busiest when I'm least working.

Alas! now pray you, / Work not so hard: I would the lightning had / Burnt up those logs that you are enjoin'd to pile! / Pray, set it down and rest you: when this burns, / 'Twill weep for having wearied you. My father / Is hard at study; pray, now, rest yourself: / He's safe for these three hours.

Oh, please, don't work so hard! I wish lightning had burnt up those logs you have been ordered to pile! Please put that down and rest. When this burns it will weep sap for having tired you. My father is busy studying. Please rest now: he's safe out of the way for the next three hours.
O most dear mistress, / The sun will set, before I shall discharge / What I must strive to do.
Oh, dearest lady, the sun will set before I finish what I have to do.
If you'll sit down, / I'll bear your logs the while. Pray give me that; / I'll carry it to the pile.
If you'll sit down, I'll carry your logs in the meantime. Please give me that; I'll take it to the pile.
No, precious creature: / I had rather crack my sinews, break my back, / Than you should such dishonour undergo, / While I sit lazy by.
No, precious creature. I would rather tear my muscles and break my back than have you suffer such dishonour while I sit by lazily.
It would become me / As well as it does you: and I should do it / With much more ease; for my good will is to it, / And yours it is against.
It would suit me as well as it suits you, and I would do it much more easily, because my heart is in it and yours is against it.
[Aside] Poor worm! thou art infected: / This visitation shows it.
Poor creature! You've caught the infection. This visit proves it.
No, noble mistress; 'tis fresh morning with me / When you are by at night. I do beseech you— / Chiefly that I might set it in my prayers— / What is your name?
No, noble lady. It's fresh morning for me when you're near, even at night. I beg you, mainly so that I can put it in my prayers, what is your name?
Miranda—O my father! / I have broke your hest to say so.
Miranda. Oh, my father! I've broken your order by telling him.

Admir'd Miranda! / Indeed, the top of admiration; worth / What's dearest to the world! Full many a lady / I have ey'd with best regard, and many a time / The harmony of their tongues hath into bondage / Brought my too diligent ear: for several virtues / Have I lik'd several women; never any / With so full soul but some defect in her / Did quarrel with the noblest grace she ow'd, / And put it to the foil: but you, O you! / So perfect and so peerless, are created / Of every creature's best.

Admired Miranda! Truly the height of admiration, worth more than the most precious things in the world! I have looked on many ladies with the greatest admiration, and many times the music of their voices has captured my too eager ear. I have liked different women for different virtues, but never one so wholeheartedly that some flaw in her didn't fight with her finest quality and spoil it. But you, oh you, so perfect and without equal, are made of the best of every creature.

I do not know / One of my sex; no woman's face remember, / Save, from my glass, mine own; nor have I seen / More that I may call men than you, good friend, / And my dear father: how features are abroad, / I am skill-less of; but, by my modesty,— / The jewel in my dower,—I would not wish / Any companion in the world but you; / Nor can imagination form a shape, / Besides yourself, to like of. But I prattle / Something too wildly, and my father's precepts / I therein do forget.

I don't know a single woman. I don't remember any woman's face except my own, from my mirror. And I haven't seen anyone I could call a man except you, good friend, and my dear father. What people look like elsewhere I have no idea. But by my modesty, the jewel of my dowry, I wouldn't wish for any companion in the world but you, and my imagination can't create any shape except yours to love. But I'm chattering too freely, and forgetting my father's instructions.

I am, in my condition, / A prince, Miranda; I do think, a king;— / I would not so!—and would no more endure / This wooden slavery than to suffer / The flesh-fly blow my mouth.—Hear my soul speak:— / The very instant that I saw you, did / My heart fly to your service; there resides, / To make me slave to it; and for your sake / Am I this patient log-man.

By rank, Miranda, I am a prince, and I think a king (I wish it weren't so!). I would no more put up with this slavery of carrying wood than let a blowfly lay eggs in my mouth. Hear my soul speak. The very moment I saw you, my heart flew to serve you. It lives there, making me its slave, and for your sake I am this patient log-carrier.

O heaven! O earth! bear witness to this sound, / And crown what I profess with kind event, / If I speak true: if hollowly, invert / What best is boded me to mischief! I, / Beyond all limit of what else i' the world, / Do love, prize, honour you.

Oh heaven, oh earth, bear witness to what I say! Crown my words with a happy outcome if I speak truly; if falsely, turn the best that's in store for me to disaster! I love, value and honour you beyond everything else in the world.
I am a fool / To weep at what I am glad of.
I'm a fool to cry at something I'm glad about.
[Aside] Fair encounter / Of two most rare affections! Heavens rain grace / On that which breeds between them!
A lovely meeting of two rare loves! May heaven rain blessings on what grows between them!

At mine unworthiness, that dare not offer / What I desire to give; and much less take / What I shall die to want. But this is trifling; / And all the more it seeks to hide itself, / The bigger bulk it shows. Hence, bashful cunning! / And prompt me, plain and holy innocence! / I am your wife, if you will marry me; / If not, I'll die your maid: to be your fellow / You may deny me; but I'll be your servant, / Whether you will or no.

Because I'm unworthy, and don't dare offer what I want to give, much less take what I'll die without. But this is nonsense: the more my love tries to hide itself, the bigger it shows. Away, shy cleverness! Guide me, plain and holy innocence! I am your wife, if you'll marry me. If not, I'll die a virgin devoted to you. You may refuse to make me your partner, but I'll be your servant, whether you want me or not.
My mistress, dearest; / And I thus humble ever.
My mistress, dearest, and I will always be as humble as this before you.
Ay, with a heart as willing / As bondage e'er of freedom: here's my hand.
Yes, with a heart as willing as a slave's is for freedom. Here's my hand.
And mine, with my heart in't: and now farewell / Till half an hour hence.
And here's mine, with my heart in it. And now goodbye until half an hour from now.
So glad of this as they, I cannot be, / Who are surpris'd withal; but my rejoicing / At nothing can be more. I'll to my book; / For yet, ere supper time, must I perform / Much business appertaining.
I can't be as glad about this as they are, since it has taken them by surprise, but nothing could make me happier. I'll go to my book, because before supper I still have a lot of work to do for this.
Tell not me:—when the butt is out we will drink / water; not a drop before: therefore bear up, and board / 'em.—Servant-monster, drink to me.
Don't tell me. When the barrel's empty we'll drink water, not a drop before. So hold steady and attack. Servant-monster, drink to me.
Servant-monster! The folly of this island! They / say there's but five upon this isle; we are three of / them; if th' other two be brained like us, the state / totters.
Servant-monster! This island is crazy! They say there are only five people on this island. We are three of them. If the other two have brains like ours, the state is tottering.
Drink, servant-monster, when I bid thee: thy / eyes are almost set in thy head.
Drink, servant-monster, when I tell you to. Your eyes are almost fixed in your head.
Where should they be set else? He were a brave / monster indeed, if they were set in his tail.
Where else would they be fixed? He'd be a fine monster indeed if they were set in his tail.

My man-monster hath drown'd his tongue in / sack: for my part, the sea cannot drown me; I swam, ere / I could recover the shore, five-and-thirty leagues, off / and on, by this light. Thou shalt be my lieutenant, / monster, or my standard.

My man-monster has drowned his tongue in sherry. As for me, the sea can't drown me. I swam thirty-five leagues, on and off, before I could reach the shore, I swear by this light. You'll be my lieutenant, monster, or my flag-bearer.
Your lieutenant, if you list; he's no standard.
Your lieutenant, if you like. He can't stand up straight like a flag.
We won't run away, Monsieur Monster.
Nor go neither: but you'll lie like dogs, and / yet say nothing neither.
Or walk either. You'll lie there like dogs and say nothing, too.
Moon-calf, speak once in thy life, if thou beest / a good moon-calf.
Moon-calf, speak once in your life, if you're a good moon-calf.
How does thy honour? Let me lick thy shoe. / I'll not serve him: he is not valiant.
How is your honour? Let me lick your shoe. I won't serve him: he's not brave.

Thou liest, most ignorant monster: I am in case / to justle a constable. Why, thou deboshed fish thou, / was there ever man a coward that hath drunk so much sack / as I to-day? Wilt thou tell a monstrous lie, being but / half fish and half a monster?

You're lying, you ignorant monster. I'm ready to take on a policeman. Why, you debauched fish, was there ever a man who was a coward after drinking as much sherry as I have today? Will you tell a monstrous lie, when you're only half a fish and half a monster?
Lo, how he mocks me! wilt thou let him, my lord?
Look how he mocks me! Will you let him, my lord?
'Lord' quoth he!—That a monster should be such / a natural!
'Lord', he says! That a monster should be such an idiot!
Lo, lo again! bite him to death, I prithee.
Look, look, again! Bite him to death, please.
Trinculo, keep a good tongue in your head: if / you prove a mutineer, the next tree! The poor monster's / my subject, and he shall not suffer indignity.
Trinculo, keep a civil tongue in your head. If you turn rebel, you'll hang from the next tree! The poor monster is my subject, and he won't be insulted.
I thank my noble lord. Wilt thou be pleas'd to / hearken once again to the suit I made to thee?
I thank my noble lord. Will you be pleased to listen again to the request I made to you?
Marry will I; kneel, and repeat it: I will stand, / and so shall Trinculo.
Indeed I will. Kneel and repeat it. I'll stand, and so will Trinculo.
As I told thee before, I am subject to a tyrant, / sorcerer, that by his cunning hath cheated me of the / island.
As I told you before, I am the subject of a tyrant, a sorcerer, who cheated me out of the island by his cunning.
Thou liest, thou jesting monkey, thou; / I would my valiant master would destroy thee; / I do not lie.
You're lying, you jesting monkey, you! I wish my brave master would destroy you. I'm not lying.
Trinculo, if you trouble him any more in his tale, / by this hand, I will supplant some of your teeth.
Trinculo, if you interrupt his story any more, by this hand, I'll knock out some of your teeth.
Mum, then, and no more.—[To CALIBAN] Proceed.
Quiet, then, and no more. Go on.
I say, by sorcery he got this isle; / From me he got it: if thy greatness will , / Revenge it on him,—for I know, thou dar'st; / But this thing dare not,—
I say he got this island by sorcery. He took it from me. If your greatness will take revenge on him for it, since I know you dare, but this thing doesn't dare...
Thou shalt be lord of it and I'll serve thee.
You'll be lord of it, and I'll serve you.
How now shall this be compassed? Canst thou / bring me to the party?
Now how can this be done? Can you take me to the man?
Yea, yea, my lord: I'll yield him thee asleep, / Where thou may'st knock a nail into his head.
Yes, yes, my lord. I'll hand him over to you asleep, where you can knock a nail into his head.

What a pied ninny's this! Thou scurvy patch!— / I do beseech thy greatness, give him blows, / And take his bottle from him: when that's gone / He shall drink nought but brine; for I'll not show him / Where the quick freshes are.

What a motley fool this is! You lousy clown! I beg your greatness, beat him and take his bottle away. When that's gone he'll drink nothing but salt water, because I won't show him where the fresh springs are.
Trinculo, run into no further danger: interrupt the / monster one word further and, by this hand, I'll turn / my mercy out o' doors, and make a stock-fish of thee.
Trinculo, don't put yourself in any more danger. Interrupt the monster one more word and, by this hand, I'll throw my mercy out of doors and beat you like dried cod.
Why, what did I? I did nothing. I'll go farther off.
Why, what did I do? I didn't do anything. I'll move further away.
Didst thou not say he lied?
Didn't you say he was lying?
Do I so? Take thou that. [Strikes TRINCULO.] As you / like this, give me the lie another time.
Am I? Take that! If you like that, call me a liar again.
I did not give the lie:—out o' your wits and / hearing too?—A pox o' your bottle! this can sack and / drinking do.—A murrain on your monster, and the devil / take your fingers!

I didn't call you a liar. Have you lost your mind and your hearing too? A plague on your bottle! This is what sherry and drinking do. A cattle disease on your monster, and the devil take your fingers!
Now, forward with your tale.—Prithee stand / further off.
Now, get on with your story. Please stand further off.
Beat him enough: after a little time, I'll beat / him too.
Beat him plenty. After a while, I'll beat him too.
Stand further off. Come on, go on.

Why, as I told thee, 'tis a custom with him / I' th' afternoon to sleep: there thou may'st brain him, / Having first seiz'd his books; or with a log / Batter his skull, or paunch him with a stake, / Or cut his wezand with thy knife. Remember / First to possess his books; for without them / He's but a sot, as I am, nor hath not / One spirit to command: they all do hate him / As rootedly as I. Burn but his books; / He has brave utensils,—for so he calls them,— / Which, when he has a house, he'll deck withal: / And that most deeply to consider is / The beauty of his daughter; he himself / Calls her a nonpareil: I never saw a woman / But only Sycorax my dam and she; / But she as far surpasseth Sycorax / As great'st does least.

Well, as I told you, it's his habit to sleep in the afternoon. There you can smash his brains in, after first seizing his books. Or batter his skull with a log, or stab him in the belly with a stake, or cut his windpipe with your knife. Remember to take his books first, because without them he's just a fool like me and hasn't a single spirit to command. They all hate him as deeply as I do. Just burn his books. He has fine furnishings, as he calls them, to decorate a house with when he has one. And what you should think about most is his daughter's beauty. He himself calls her a wonder without equal. I've never seen a woman except my mother Sycorax and her, but she is as far beyond Sycorax as the greatest is beyond the least.
Is it so brave a lass?
Is she such a fine girl?
Ay, lord: she will become thy bed, I warrant, / And bring thee forth brave brood.
Yes, lord. She'll suit your bed, I promise, and give you fine children.
Monster, I will kill this man; his daughter and I / will be king and queen,—save our graces!—and Trinculo / and thyself shall be viceroys. Dost thou like the plot, / Trinculo?
Monster, I will kill this man. His daughter and I will be king and queen (God save our majesties!), and Trinculo and you will be my deputies. Do you like the plan, Trinculo?
Give me thy hand: I am sorry I beat thee; but / while thou livest, keep a good tongue in thy head.
Give me your hand. I'm sorry I hit you, but as long as you live, keep a civil tongue in your head.
Within this half hour will he be asleep; / Wilt thou destroy him then?
Within this half hour he'll be asleep. Will you kill him then?
This will I tell my master.
Thou mak'st me merry: I am full of pleasure. / Let us be jocund: will you troll the catch / You taught me but while-ere?
You make me merry. I'm full of joy. Let's be cheerful. Will you sing the round you taught me just now?
At thy request, monster, I will do reason, any / reason. Come on, Trinculo, let us sing. / [Sings] / Flout 'em and scout 'em; and scout 'em and flout 'em: / Thought is free.
Since you ask, monster, I'll do anything reasonable, anything. Come on, Trinculo, let's sing. Mock them and jeer them, jeer them and mock them: thoughts are free.
This is the tune of our catch, played by the / picture of Nobody.
This is the tune of our song, played by the picture of Nobody.
If thou beest a man, show thyself in thy / likeness: if thou beest a devil, take't as thou list.
If you're a man, show yourself in your true shape. If you're a devil, do as you like.
He that dies pays all debts: I defy thee.—Mercy / upon us!
A man who dies pays all his debts. I defy you. Mercy on us!

Be not afeard: the isle is full of noises, / Sounds, and sweet airs, that give delight, and hurt not. / Sometimes a thousand twangling instruments / Will hum about mine ears; and sometimes voices, / That, if I then had wak'd after long sleep, / Will make me sleep again: and then, in dreaming, / The clouds methought would open and show riches / Ready to drop upon me; that, when I wak'd, / I cried to dream again.

Don't be afraid. The island is full of noises, sounds and sweet tunes that give delight and do no harm. Sometimes a thousand twanging instruments hum around my ears, and sometimes voices that, if I had just woken from a long sleep, would make me sleep again. And then, while dreaming, I thought the clouds would open and show riches ready to drop on me, so that when I woke I cried to dream again.
This will prove a brave kingdom to me, where I / shall have my music for nothing.
This will be a fine kingdom for me, where I'll have my music for free.
That shall be by and by: I remember the story.
That will be soon. I remember the plan.
The sound is going away: let's follow it, and / after do our work.
The sound is moving away. Let's follow it, and do our job afterwards.
Lead, monster: we'll follow.—I would I could see / this taborer! he lays it on. Wilt come?
Lead on, monster. We'll follow. I wish I could see this drummer! He's really going at it. Are you coming?
By'r lakin, I can go no further, sir; / My old bones ache: here's a maze trod, indeed, / Through forth-rights and meanders! By your patience, / I needs must rest me.
By Our Lady, I can't go any further, sir. My old bones ache. We've walked through a real maze of straight paths and winding ones! With your permission, I must rest.

Old lord, I cannot blame thee, / Who am myself attach'd with weariness / To th' dulling of my spirits: sit down, and rest. / Even here I will put off my hope, and keep it / No longer for my flatterer: he is drown'd / Whom thus we stray to find; and the sea mocks / Our frustrate search on land. Well, let him go.

Old lord, I can't blame you, since I'm worn out myself, to the point of numbness. Sit down and rest. Right here I'll give up my hope and keep it no longer to flatter me. The one we wander about looking for is drowned, and the sea mocks our useless search on land. Well, let him go.
[Aside to SEBASTIAN] I am right glad that he's / so out of hope. / Do not, for one repulse, forgo the purpose / That you resolv'd to effect.
I'm very glad he's lost hope. Don't give up the plan you decided to carry out just because of one setback.
[Aside to ANTONIO] The next advantage / Will we take throughly.
We'll take the next opportunity thoroughly.
[Aside to SEBASTIAN] Let it be to-night; / For, now they are oppress'd with travel, they / Will not, nor cannot, use such vigilance / As when they are fresh.
Let it be tonight. Now that they're worn out with walking, they won't and can't be as watchful as when they're fresh.
[Aside to ANTONIO] I say, to-night: no more.
What harmony is this? my good friends, hark!
What music is this? My good friends, listen!
Give us kind keepers, heavens! What were these?
Heaven, give us kind guardian angels! What were those?
A living drollery. Now I will believe / That there are unicorns; that in Arabia / There is one tree, the phoenix' throne; one phoenix / At this hour reigning there.
A live puppet show. Now I'll believe that there are unicorns, and that in Arabia there is one tree that's the phoenix's throne, with one phoenix reigning there right now.
I'll believe both; / And what does else want credit, come to me, / And I'll be sworn 'tis true: travellers ne'er did lie, / Though fools at home condemn them.
I'll believe both. And anything else that's hard to believe, bring it to me and I'll swear it's true. Travellers never lied, though fools at home condemn them.

If in Naples / I should report this now, would they believe me? / If I should say, I saw such islanders,— / For, certes, these are people of the island,— / Who, though, they are of monstrous shape, yet, note, / Their manners are more gentle-kind than of / Our human generation you shall find / Many, nay, almost any.

If I reported this in Naples now, would they believe me? If I said I'd seen islanders like these (because surely these are people of the island), who, though they are monstrous in shape, have manners, notice, more gentle and kind than you'll find in many of our human race, in fact almost any.
[Aside] Honest lord, / Thou hast said well; for some of you there present / Are worse than devils.
Honest lord, you've said well, because some of you standing there are worse than devils.
I cannot too much muse / Such shapes, such gesture, and such sound, expressing,— / Although they want the use of tongue,—a kind / Of excellent dumb discourse.
I can't marvel enough at such shapes, such gestures and such sounds, expressing, even though they can't speak, a kind of excellent silent conversation.
Save your praise until the end.
No matter, since / They have left their viands behind; for we have stomachs.— / Will't please you taste of what is here?
No matter, since they've left their food behind, and we're hungry. Would you like to taste some of this?

Faith, sir, you need not fear. When we were boys, / Who would believe that there were mountaineers / Dewlapp'd like bulls, whose throats had hanging at them / Wallets of flesh? or that there were such men / Whose heads stood in their breasts? which now we find / Each putter-out of five for one will bring us / Good warrant of.

Honestly, sir, you needn't be afraid. When we were boys, who would have believed that there were mountain men with folds of skin hanging from their throats like bulls, like bags of flesh? Or that there were men whose heads were in their chests? Yet now every traveller who bets five to one on coming home safely brings us proof of these things.
I will stand to, and feed, / Although my last; no matter, since I feel / The best is past.—Brother, my lord the duke, / Stand to and do as we.
I will step up and eat, even if it's my last meal. It doesn't matter, since I feel the best of my life is over. Brother, my lord the Duke, step up and do as we do.

You are three men of sin, whom Destiny, / That hath to instrument this lower world / And what is in't,—the never-surfeited sea / Hath caused to belch up you; and on this island / Where man doth not inhabit; you 'mongst men / Being most unfit to live. I have made you mad:

You are three sinful men. Destiny, which uses this lower world and everything in it as its instrument, has made the never-satisfied sea belch you up, and onto this island where no man lives, since you are the most unfit of all men to live. I have made you mad.

And even with such-like valour men hang and drown / Their proper selves. You fools! I and my fellows / Are ministers of fate: the elements / Of whom your swords are temper'd may as well / Wound the loud winds, or with bemock'd-at stabs / Kill the still-closing waters, as diminish / One dowle that's in my plume; my fellow-ministers / Are like invulnerable. If you could hurt, / Your swords are now too massy for your strengths, / And will not be uplifted. But, remember— / For that's my business to you,—that you three / From Milan did supplant good Prospero; / Expos'd unto the sea, which hath requit it, / Him, and his innocent child: for which foul deed / The powers, delaying, not forgetting, have / Incens'd the seas and shores, yea, all the creatures, / Against your peace. Thee of thy son, Alonso, / They have bereft; and do pronounce, by me / Lingering perdition,—worse than any death / Can be at once,—shall step by step attend / You and your ways; whose wraths to guard you from— / Which here, in this most desolate isle, else falls / Upon your heads,—is nothing but heart-sorrow, / And a clear life ensuing.

And it is with this kind of courage that men hang and drown themselves. You fools! My fellows and I are agents of fate. The metal your swords are made of could as easily wound the loud winds, or kill the waters that always close up again with stabs they laugh at, as cut one fibre of my feathers. My fellow agents are just as invulnerable. Even if you could hurt us, your swords are now too heavy for your strength, and you can't lift them. But remember, because that's my business with you, that you three overthrew good Prospero in Milan. You put him and his innocent child out on the sea, which has now paid you back. For that foul deed the heavenly powers, which delay but do not forget, have stirred up the seas and shores, and every creature, against your peace. Alonso, they have taken your son from you, and through me they declare that a slow ruin, worse than any sudden death, will follow you step by step wherever you go. The only protection from their anger, which will otherwise fall on your heads on this desolate island, is true repentance and a pure life from now on.

[Aside] Bravely the figure of this harpy hast thou / Perform'd, my Ariel; a grace it had, devouring; / Of my instruction hast thou nothing bated / In what thou hadst to say: so, with good life / And observation strange, my meaner ministers / Their several kinds have done. My high charms work, / And these mine enemies are all knit up / In their distractions; they now are in my power; / And in these fits I leave them, while I visit / Young Ferdinand,—whom they suppose is drown'd,— / And his and mine lov'd darling.

You played the part of this harpy splendidly, my Ariel. You had a devouring grace. You left out nothing of what I told you to say. And my lesser spirits have played their different parts with lifelike skill and wonderful care. My powerful spells are working, and these enemies of mine are all tied up in their madness. Now they're in my power. I'll leave them in these fits while I visit young Ferdinand, whom they think is drowned, and his and my beloved darling.
I' the name of something holy, sir, why stand you / In this strange stare?
In the name of all that's holy, sir, why are you standing there staring like this?

O, it is monstrous! monstrous! / Methought the billows spoke, and told me of it; / The winds did sing it to me; and the thunder, / That deep and dreadful organ-pipe, pronounc'd / The name of Prosper: it did bass my trespass. / Therefore my son i' th' ooze is bedded; and / I'll seek him deeper than e'er plummet sounded, / And with him there lie mudded.

Oh, it's monstrous, monstrous! I thought the waves spoke and told me of it. The winds sang it to me, and the thunder, that deep and dreadful organ pipe, pronounced the name of Prospero. It sang out my crime in a bass voice. That's why my son lies buried in the mud of the sea bed, and I'll look for him deeper than any plumb line ever sank, and lie there with him in the mud.
But one fiend at a time, / I'll fight their legions o'er.
If they come one fiend at a time, I'll fight their whole armies.

All three of them are desperate: their great guilt, / Like poison given to work a great time after, / Now 'gins to bite the spirits. I do beseech you / That are of suppler joints, follow them swiftly / And hinder them from what this ecstasy / May now provoke them to.

All three of them are desperate. Their great guilt, like a poison designed to work long afterwards, is starting to bite their souls. I beg you, who have more flexible joints, follow them quickly and stop them doing what this madness may drive them to.

If I have too austerely punish'd you, / Your compensation makes amends: for / Have given you here a third of mine own life, / Or that for which I live; who once again / I tender to thy hand: all thy vexations / Were but my trials of thy love, and thou / Hast strangely stood the test: here, afore Heaven, / I ratify this my rich gift. O Ferdinand! / Do not smile at me that I boast her off, / For thou shalt find she will outstrip all praise, / And make it halt behind her.

If I have punished you too harshly, your reward makes up for it, because I have given you here a third of my own life, or rather the thing I live for. I hand her over to you once again. All your hardships were only my tests of your love, and you have passed them wonderfully. Here, before heaven, I confirm this rich gift of mine. Oh Ferdinand, don't smile at me for boasting about her, because you'll find she outruns all praise and leaves it limping behind her.
I do believe it / Against an oracle.
I would believe that even if an oracle said otherwise.

Then, as my gift and thine own acquisition / Worthily purchas'd, take my daughter: but / If thou dost break her virgin knot before / All sanctimonious ceremonies may / With full and holy rite be minister'd, / No sweet aspersion shall the heavens let fall / To make this contract grow; but barren hate, / Sour-ey'd disdain, and discord, shall bestrew / The union of your bed with weeds so loathly / That you shall hate it both: therefore take heed, / As Hymen's lamps shall light you.

Then take my daughter, as my gift and as your own prize, which you have worthily won. But if you break her virginity before all the holy ceremonies have been performed with full and sacred rites, the heavens will let no sweet blessing fall to make this marriage grow. Instead barren hatred, sour-eyed contempt and quarrelling will scatter such hateful weeds over your marriage bed that you will both loathe it. So be careful, as you hope the god of marriage will light your way.

As I hope / For quiet days, fair issue, and long life, / With such love as 'tis now, the murkiest den, / The most opportune place, the strong'st suggestion / Our worser genius can, shall never melt / Mine honour into lust, to take away / The edge of that day's celebration, / When I shall think, or Phoebus' steeds are founder'd, / Or Night kept chain'd below.

As I hope for peaceful days, fine children and a long life, with love like ours now, not the darkest cave, the most convenient place, nor the strongest temptation my worse angel can offer will ever melt my honour into lust and blunt the joy of our wedding day, when I'll think either that the sun god's horses have gone lame or that Night is chained underground.
Fairly spoke: / Sit, then, and talk with her, she is thine own. / What, Ariel! my industrious servant, Ariel!
Nicely said. Sit, then, and talk with her: she is yours. Ariel! My hard-working servant, Ariel!
What would my potent master? here I am.
What does my powerful master want? Here I am.

Thou and thy meaner fellows your last service / Did worthily perform; and I must use you / In such another trick. Go bring the rabble, / O'er whom I give thee power, here to this place; / Incite them to quick motion; for I must / Bestow upon the eyes of this young couple / Some vanity of mine art: it is my promise, / And they expect it from me.

You and your lesser companions did your last job well, and I must use you in another trick like it. Go and bring the crowd of spirits I've given you power over to this place. Make them move quickly, because I must show the eyes of this young couple some little display of my art. I promised it, and they expect it of me.
Yes, in the blink of an eye.
Before you can say 'Come' and 'Go,' / And breathe twice; and cry 'so, so,' / Each one, tripping on his toe, / Will be here with mop and mow. / Do you love me, master? no?
Before you can say 'come' and 'go', and breathe twice, and cry 'so, so', each one, tripping on tiptoe, will be here pulling faces. Do you love me, master? No?
Dearly, my delicate Ariel. Do not approach / Till thou dost hear me call.
Dearly, my delicate Ariel. Don't come near until you hear me call.
Look, thou be true; do not give dalliance / Too much the rein: the strongest oaths are straw / To th' fire i' the blood: be more abstemious, / Or else good night your vow!
Make sure you keep your word. Don't give your flirting too much rein. The strongest oaths are straw to the fire in the blood. Hold back more, or else goodbye to your vow!
I warrant you, sir; / The white-cold virgin snow upon my heart / Abates the ardour of my liver.
I promise you, sir, the cold white virgin snow of her on my heart cools the heat of my passion.
Well.— / Now come, my Ariel! bring a corollary, / Rather than want a spirit: appear, and pertly. / No tongue! all eyes! be silent.
Good. Now come, my Ariel! Bring one spirit too many rather than one too few. Appear, and be quick. No talking! All eyes! Be silent.

Ceres, most bounteous lady, thy rich leas / Of wheat, rye, barley, vetches, oats, and peas; / Thy turfy mountains, where live nibbling sheep, / And flat meads thatch'd with stover, them to keep; / Thy banks with pioned and twilled brims, / Which spongy April at thy hest betrims, / To make cold nymphs chaste crowns; and thy broom groves, / Whose shadow the dismissed bachelor loves, / Being lass-lorn: thy pole-clipt vineyard; / And thy sea-marge, sterile and rocky-hard, / Where thou thyself dost air: the Queen o' the sky, / Whose watery arch and messenger am I, / Bids thee leave these; and with her sovereign grace, / Here on this grass-plot, in this very place, / To come and sport; her peacocks fly amain: / Approach, rich Ceres, her to entertain.

Ceres, most generous lady, your rich fields of wheat, rye, barley, vetch, oats and peas; your grassy hills where nibbling sheep live, and flat meadows covered with hay to feed them; your riverbanks with dug-out and woven edges, which rainy April decorates with flowers at your command to make chaste crowns for cold nymphs; your groves of broom, whose shade the rejected young man loves when he has lost his girl; your vineyard with its staked vines; and your seashore, barren and rocky, where you yourself take the air: the Queen of the sky, whose rainbow and messenger I am, tells you to leave all these and, by her royal favour, come and play here on this patch of grass, in this very place. Her peacocks are flying fast. Come near, rich Ceres, to welcome her.

Hail, many-colour'd messenger, that ne'er / Dost disobey the wife of Jupiter; / Who with thy saffron wings upon my flowers / Diffusest honey drops, refreshing showers: / And with each end of thy blue bow dost crown / My bosky acres and my unshrubb'd down, / Rich scarf to my proud earth; why hath thy queen / Summon'd me hither to this short-grass'd green?

Greetings, many-coloured messenger, who never disobeys the wife of Jupiter. With your saffron wings you scatter honey drops and refreshing showers on my flowers, and with each end of your blue bow you crown my wooded acres and my bare hills, a rich scarf for my proud earth. Why has your queen called me here to this short-grassed lawn?
A contract of true love to celebrate, / And some donation freely to estate / On the blest lovers.
To celebrate a contract of true love, and to give a gift freely to the blessed lovers.

Tell me, heavenly bow, / If Venus or her son, as thou dost know, / Do now attend the queen? Since they did plot / The means that dusky Dis my daughter got, / Her and her blind boy's scandal'd company / I have forsworn.

Tell me, heavenly rainbow, as far as you know, are Venus or her son now with the Queen? Since they plotted the way gloomy Pluto got my daughter, I have sworn to avoid her company and her blind boy's disgraceful company.

Of her society / Be not afraid. I met her deity / Cutting the clouds towards Paphos and her son / Dove-drawn with her. Here thought they to have done / Some wanton charm upon this man and maid, / Whose vows are, that no bed-rite shall be paid / Till Hymen's torch be lighted; but in vain. / Mars's hot minion is return'd again; / Her waspish-headed son has broke his arrows, / Swears he will shoot no more, but play with sparrows, / And be a boy right out.

Don't be afraid of meeting her. I met the goddess cutting through the clouds towards Paphos, with her son, in her chariot drawn by doves. They planned to cast some lustful spell on this man and girl, who have vowed that no wedding-night rites will be paid until the torch of the marriage god is lit. But it was useless. Mars's hot lover has gone back home. Her hot-tempered son has broken his arrows, swears he'll shoot no more but play with sparrows, and be a plain boy.
Highest Queen of State, / Great Juno comes; I know her by her gait.
The highest Queen of all, great Juno, is coming. I know her by her walk.
How does my bounteous sister? Go with me / To bless this twain, that they may prosperous be, / And honour'd in their issue.
How is my generous sister? Come with me to bless this couple, so that they may prosper and be honoured in their children.
Honour, riches, marriage-blessing, / Long continuance, and increasing, / Hourly joys be still upon you! / Juno sings her blessings on you.
Honour, riches, the blessing of marriage, long life and growing families, may joys be with you every hour! Juno sings her blessings on you.

Earth's increase, foison plenty, / Barns and garners never empty; / Vines with clust'ring bunches growing; / Plants with goodly burden bowing; / Spring come to you at the farthest, / In the very end of harvest! / Scarcity and want shall shun you; / Ceres' blessing so is on you.

The earth's harvest and plenty of produce, barns and granaries never empty, vines growing with clusters of grapes, plants bending under their fine loads! May spring come back to you at the latest as soon as harvest ends! Scarcity and need will avoid you. This is Ceres' blessing on you.
This is a most majestic vision, and / Harmonious charmingly; may I be bold / To think these spirits?
This is a most majestic vision, and charmingly harmonious. May I be so bold as to think these are spirits?
Spirits, which by mine art / I have from their confines call'd to enact / My present fancies.
Spirits, which I have called by my art from where they are kept to act out my present fancies.
Let me live here ever: / So rare a wonder'd father and a wise, / Makes this place Paradise.
Let me live here for ever. Such a rare, wonder-working and wise father makes this place Paradise.
Sweet now, silence! / Juno and Ceres whisper seriously, / There's something else to do: hush, and be mute, / Or else our spell is marr'd.
Sweet one, quiet now! Juno and Ceres are whispering seriously. There's something more to come. Hush and be silent, or our spell will be spoiled.

You nymphs, call'd Naiads, of the windring brooks, / With your sedg'd crowns and ever-harmless looks, / Leave your crisp channels, and on this green land / Answer your summons: Juno does command. / Come, temperate nymphs, and help to celebrate / A contract of true love: be not too late.

You nymphs, called Naiads, of the winding streams, with your crowns of reeds and your ever-innocent looks, leave your rippling channels and answer your summons on this green land. Juno commands it. Come, chaste nymphs, and help to celebrate a contract of true love. Don't be late.
You sun-burn'd sicklemen, of August weary, / Come hither from the furrow, and be merry: / Make holiday: your rye-straw hats put on, / And these fresh nymphs encounter every one / In country footing.
You sunburnt harvesters, tired of August, come here from the furrows and be merry. Take a holiday. Put on your straw hats and join these fresh nymphs, every one of you, in a country dance.
[Aside] I had forgot that foul conspiracy / Of the beast Caliban and his confederates / Against my life: the minute of their plot / Is almost come. [To the Spirits.] Well done! avoid; no / more!
I had forgotten that foul plot of the beast Caliban and his accomplices against my life. The time set for their plot has almost come. Well done! Go away! No more!
This is strange: your father's in some passion / That works him strongly.
This is strange. Your father is in some passion that is shaking him badly.
Never till this day / Saw I him touch'd with anger so distemper'd.
I have never seen him so moved by such violent anger until today.

You do look, my son, in a mov'd sort, / As if you were dismay'd: be cheerful, sir: / Our revels now are ended. These our actors, / As I foretold you, were all spirits and / Are melted into air, into thin air: / And, like the baseless fabric of this vision, / The cloud-capp'd towers, the gorgeous palaces, / The solemn temples, the great globe itself, / Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolve / And, like this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded with a sleep.—Sir, I am vex'd: / Bear with my weakness; my old brain is troubled. / Be not disturb'd with my infirmity. / If you be pleas'd, retire into my cell / And there repose: a turn or two I'll walk, / To still my beating mind.

You look upset, my son, as if you were alarmed. Cheer up, sir. Our entertainment is over now. These actors of ours, as I told you, were all spirits and have melted into air, into thin air. And, like the baseless structure of this vision, the cloud-topped towers, the splendid palaces, the solemn temples, the great globe itself, yes, and everyone who lives on it, will dissolve, and, just as this insubstantial show has faded, leave not a wisp of cloud behind. We are made of the same stuff as dreams, and our little life is surrounded by a sleep. Sir, I am troubled. Bear with my weakness: my old brain is disturbed. Don't be worried by my frailty. If you like, go into my cave and rest there. I'll walk around a little to calm my racing mind.
Come, with a thought.—[To them.] I thank thee: / Ariel, come!
Come as quick as thought. I thank you. Ariel, come!
Thy thoughts I cleave to. What's thy pleasure?
I cling to your thoughts. What do you want?
Spirit, / We must prepare to meet with Caliban.
Spirit, we must get ready to meet Caliban.
Ay, my commander; when I presented Ceres, / I thought to have told thee of it: but I fear'd / Lest I might anger thee.
Yes, my commander. When I played Ceres I meant to tell you about it, but I was afraid I might make you angry.
Say again, where didst thou leave these varlets?
Tell me again, where did you leave these rogues?

I told you, sir, they were red-hot with drinking; / So full of valour that they smote the air / For breathing in their faces; beat the ground / For kissing of their feet; yet always bending / Towards their project. Then I beat my tabor; / At which, like unback'd colts, they prick'd their ears, / Advanc'd their eyelids, lifted up their noses / As they smelt music: so I charm'd their ears, / That calf-like they my lowing follow'd through / Tooth'd briers, sharp furzes, pricking goss and thorns, / Which enter'd their frail shins: at last I left them / I' the filthy-mantled pool beyond your cell, / There dancing up to the chins, that the foul lake / O'erstunk their feet.

I told you, sir, they were red-hot with drinking, so full of courage that they struck the air for breathing in their faces and beat the ground for kissing their feet, yet always heading towards their plan. Then I beat my drum, and at that, like unbroken colts, they pricked up their ears, opened their eyes wide and lifted their noses as if they could smell music. I charmed their ears so that they followed my mooing like calves, through toothed briars, sharp gorse, prickly furze and thorns, which pierced their tender shins. At last I left them in the scum-covered pond beyond your cave, dancing there up to their chins, so that the stinking pool smelled worse than their feet.
This was well done, my bird. / Thy shape invisible retain thou still: / The trumpery in my house, go bring it hither / For stale to catch these thieves.
That was well done, my bird. Keep your invisible shape. Go and bring the showy clothes from my house here, as bait to catch these thieves.

A devil, a born devil, on whose nature / Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, / Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost; / And as with age his body uglier grows, / So his mind cankers. I will plague them all, / Even to roaring.

A devil, a born devil, whose nature can never be improved by upbringing. All my efforts, taken out of kindness, are all lost, completely lost. And as his body grows uglier with age, so his mind rots. I will torment them all, until they roar.
Come, hang them on this line.
Come on, hang them on this line.
Pray you, tread softly, that the blind mole may not / Hear a foot fall: we now are near his cell.
Please, walk softly, so that even the blind mole can't hear a footstep. We're near his cave now.
Monster, your fairy, which you say is a harmless / fairy, has done little better than played the / Jack with us.
Monster, your fairy, which you say is a harmless fairy, has done little more than play the fool with us.
Monster, I do smell all horse-piss; at which my / nose is in great indignation.
Monster, I smell all of horse piss, and my nose is very offended by it.
So is mine.—Do you hear, monster? If I should / take a displeasure against you, look you,—
So is mine. Do you hear, monster? If I took a dislike to you, look out...
Thou wert but a lost monster.
Good my lord, give me thy favour still: / Be patient, for the prize I'll bring thee to / Shall hoodwink this mischance: therefore speak softly; / All's hush'd as midnight yet.
My good lord, keep favouring me. Be patient, because the prize I'll lead you to will make you forget this bad luck. So speak quietly. Everything's still as hushed as midnight.
Ay, but to lose our bottles in the pool!—
Yes, but to lose our bottles in the pond!
There is not only disgrace and dishonour in / that, monster, but an infinite loss.
There's not only shame and dishonour in that, monster, but an infinite loss.
That's more to me than my wetting: yet this is / your harmless fairy, monster.
That matters more to me than my soaking. And yet this is your harmless fairy, monster.
I will fetch off my bottle, though I be o'er / ears for my labour.
I'll get my bottle back, even if I'm in over my ears for my trouble.

Prithee, my king, be quiet. Seest thou here, / This is the mouth o' the cell: no noise, and enter. / Do that good mischief which may make this island / Thine own for ever, and I, thy Caliban, / For aye thy foot-licker.

Please, my king, be quiet. Do you see this? This is the mouth of the cave. No noise, and go in. Do that good wickedness that will make this island yours for ever, and me, your Caliban, your foot-licker for ever.
Give me thy hand: I do begin to have bloody / thoughts.
Give me your hand. I'm starting to have bloody thoughts.
O King Stephano! O peer! O worthy Stephano! / Look what a wardrobe here is for thee!
Oh, King Stephano! Oh, lord! Oh, worthy Stephano! Look what a wardrobe there is here for you!
Let it alone, thou fool; it is but trash.
Leave it alone, you fool. It's only rubbish.
O, ho, monster! we know what belongs to a / frippery.—O King Stephano!
Oh, ho, monster! We know what belongs in a second-hand clothes shop. Oh, King Stephano!
Put off that gown, Trinculo; by this hand, I'll / have that gown.
Take off that gown, Trinculo. By this hand, I'll have that gown.

The dropsy drown this fool! What do you mean / To dote thus on such luggage? Let's along, / And do the murder first. If he awake, / From toe to crown he'll fill our skins with pinches; / Make us strange stuff.

May the dropsy drown this fool! What do you mean by drooling over such junk? Let's go and do the murder first. If he wakes, he'll fill our skins with pinches from head to toe and turn us into strange stuff.
Be you quiet, monster.—Mistress line, is not / this my jerkin? Now is the jerkin under the line: now, / jerkin, you are like to lose your hair, and prove a bald / jerkin.
You be quiet, monster. Mistress Line, isn't this my jacket? Now the jacket is under the line. Now, jacket, you're likely to lose your hair and turn out to be a bald jacket.
Do, do: we steal by line and level, an't like / your Grace.
Go on, go on. We steal by the plumb line and the level, if it please your Grace.

I thank thee for that jest: here's a garment / for't: wit shall not go unrewarded while I am king of / this country: 'Steal by line and level,' is an excellent / pass of pate: there's another garment for't.
Thank you for that joke. Here's a garment for it. Wit won't go unrewarded while I'm king of this country. 'Steal by line and level' is an excellent piece of wit. There's another garment for it.
Monster, come, put some lime upon your fingers, / and away with the rest.
Monster, come on, put some glue on your fingers and take the rest.
I will have none on't. We shall lose our time, / And all be turn'd to barnacles, or to apes / With foreheads villainous low.
I'll have none of it. We'll waste our time and all be turned into barnacle geese, or into apes with horribly low foreheads.
Monster, lay-to your fingers: help to bear this / away where my hogshead of wine is, or I'll turn you out / of my kingdom. Go to; carry this.
Monster, put your fingers to work. Help carry this to where my barrel of wine is, or I'll throw you out of my kingdom. Come on, carry this.
Fury, Fury! There, Tyrant, there! hark, hark!
Fury, Fury! There, Tyrant, there! Listen, listen!
Go, charge my goblins that they grind their joints / With dry convulsions; shorten up their sinews / With aged cramps, and more pinch-spotted make them / Than pard, or cat o' mountain.
Go, order my goblins to grind their joints with dry convulsions, shrink their muscles with old people's cramps, and make them more spotted with pinches than a leopard or a wildcat.
Let them be hunted soundly. At this hour / Lies at my mercy all mine enemies; / Shortly shall all my labours end, and thou / Shalt have the air at freedom; for a little / Follow, and do me service.
Let them be hunted thoroughly. At this moment all my enemies are at my mercy. Soon all my work will be finished, and you will have the freedom of the air. For a little longer, follow me and serve me.
Now does my project gather to a head: / My charms crack not; my spirits obey, and time / Goes upright with his carriage. How's the day?
Now my plan is coming to its climax. My spells hold, my spirits obey, and time walks upright under its load. What time is it?
On the sixth hour; at which time, my lord, / You said our work should cease.
Nearly six o'clock, the time, my lord, when you said our work would end.
I did say so, / When first I rais'd the tempest. Say, my spirit, / How fares the King and 's followers?
I did say so, when I first raised the storm. Tell me, my spirit, how are the King and his followers?

Confin'd together / In the same fashion as you gave in charge; / Just as you left them: all prisoners, sir, / In the line-grove which weather-fends your cell; / They cannot budge till your release. The king, / His brother, and yours, abide all three distracted, / And the remainder mourning over them, / Brim full of sorrow and dismay; but chiefly / Him you term'd, sir, 'the good old lord, Gonzalo': / His tears run down his beard, like winter's drops / From eaves of reeds; your charm so strongly works them, / That if you now beheld them, your affections / Would become tender.

Imprisoned together just as you ordered, exactly as you left them. They're all prisoners, sir, in the grove of lime trees that shelters your cave from the weather. They can't move until you release them. The King, his brother and yours are all three out of their minds, and the rest are mourning over them, brimming with sorrow and alarm, but most of all the one you called, sir, 'the good old lord, Gonzalo'. His tears run down his beard like winter rain from a thatched roof. Your spell works on them so strongly that if you saw them now, your feelings would soften.
Mine would, sir, were I human.
Mine would, sir, if I were human.

And mine shall. / Hast thou, which art but air, a touch, a feeling / Of their afflictions, and shall not myself, / One of their kind, that relish all as sharply, / Passion as they, be kindlier mov'd than thou art? / Though with their high wrongs I am struck to the quick, / Yet with my nobler reason 'gainst my fury / Do I take part: the rarer action is / In virtue than in vengeance: they being penitent, / The sole drift of my purpose doth extend / Not a frown further. Go release them, Ariel. / My charms I'll break, their senses I'll restore, / And they shall be themselves.

And mine will. If you, who are only air, have a sense and feeling of their sufferings, shouldn't I, one of their own kind, who feel everything as sharply and suffer as they do, be more kindly moved than you? Although their great wrongs have cut me to the quick, I take the side of my nobler reason against my fury. It is a rarer act to forgive than to take revenge. Since they are sorry, my purpose goes not one frown further. Go and release them, Ariel. I'll break my spells and restore their senses, and they'll be themselves again.

Ye elves of hills, brooks, standing lakes, and groves; / And ye that on the sands with printless foot / Do chase the ebbing Neptune, and do fly him / When he comes back; you demi-puppets that / By moonshine do the green sour ringlets make, / Whereof the ewe not bites; and you whose pastime / Is to make midnight mushrooms, that rejoice / To hear the solemn curfew; by whose aid,— / Weak masters though ye be,—I have bedimm'd / The noontide sun, call'd forth the mutinous winds, / And 'twixt the green sea and the azur'd vault / Set roaring war: to the dread rattling thunder / Have I given fire, and rifted Jove's stout oak / With his own bolt: the strong-bas'd promontory / Have I made shake; and by the spurs pluck'd up / The pine and cedar: graves at my command / Have wak'd their sleepers, op'd, and let them forth / By my so potent art. But this rough magic / I here abjure; and, when I have requir'd / Some heavenly music,—which even now I do,— / To work mine end upon their senses that / This airy charm is for, I'll break my staff, / Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, / And deeper than did ever plummet sound / I'll drown my book.

You elves of the hills, the brooks, the still lakes and the woods, and you who chase the ebbing sea on the sands without leaving a footprint and run from it when it comes back; you tiny puppet-like fairies who make the sour green rings in the grass by moonlight, which the ewes won't eat; and you whose hobby is to make mushrooms grow at midnight, who love to hear the solemn evening bell: with your help, weak as you are, I have darkened the midday sun, called up the rebellious winds, and set a roaring war between the green sea and the blue sky. I have set fire to the dreadful rattling thunder and split Jove's sturdy oak with his own lightning bolt. I have made the firmly rooted headland shake and pulled up pines and cedars by their roots. At my command graves have woken their sleepers, opened, and let them out, by my powerful art. But I here give up this rough magic. And when I have called for some heavenly music, which I'm doing now, to work my purpose on the senses of those this airy spell is meant for, I'll break my staff, bury it several fathoms deep in the earth, and drown my book deeper than any plumb line ever sank.

A solemn air, and the best comforter / To an unsettled fancy, cure thy brains, / Now useless, boil'd within thy skull! There stand, / For you are spell-stopp'd. / Holy Gonzalo, honourable man, / Mine eyes, even sociable to the show of thine, / Fall fellowly drops. The charm dissolves apace; / And as the morning steals upon the night, / Melting the darkness, so their rising senses / Begin to chase the ignorant fumes that mantle / Their clearer reason.—O good Gonzalo! / My true preserver, and a loyal sir / To him thou follow'st, I will pay thy graces / Home, both in word and deed.—Most cruelly / Didst thou, Alonso, use me and my daughter: / Thy brother was a furtherer in the act;— / Thou'rt pinch'd for't now, Sebastian.—Flesh and blood, / You, brother mine, that entertain'd ambition, / Expell'd remorse and nature, who, with Sebastian,— / Whose inward pinches therefore are most strong,— / Would here have kill'd your king; I do forgive thee, / Unnatural though thou art! Their understanding / Begins to swell, and the approaching tide / Will shortly fill the reasonable shores / That now lie foul and muddy. Not one of them / That yet looks on me, or would know me.—Ariel, / Fetch me the hat and rapier in my cell:—

May a solemn tune, the best comfort for a disturbed mind, cure your brains, which are useless now and boiling inside your skull! Stand there, because you are frozen by a spell. Holy Gonzalo, honourable man, my eyes, in sympathy with the sight of yours, shed tears to keep them company. The spell is dissolving fast, and as the morning creeps up on the night and melts the darkness, so their returning senses begin to chase away the fog of confusion that covers their clearer reason. Oh, good Gonzalo, my true saviour and a loyal servant to the master you follow, I will repay your kindnesses in full, in words and deeds. Alonso, you treated me and my daughter most cruelly. Your brother helped you do it. You're tormented for it now, Sebastian. And you, my own flesh and blood, my brother, who welcomed ambition and drove out pity and natural feeling, who, with Sebastian (whose inner torments are therefore the strongest), would have killed your king here: I forgive you, unnatural as you are! Their understanding is starting to rise, and the coming tide will soon fill the shores of their reason, which now lie foul and muddy. Not one of them is yet looking at me or would recognise me. Ariel, fetch me the hat and sword from my cave.
I will discase me, and myself present, / As I was sometime Milan.—Quickly, spirit; / Thou shalt ere long be free.
I'll take off these robes and present myself as I used to be when I was Duke of Milan. Quickly, spirit. You'll soon be free.

Where the bee sucks, there suck I: / In a cowslip's bell I lie; / There I couch when owls do cry. / On the bat's back I do fly / After summer merrily: / Merrily, merrily shall I live now / Under the blossom that hangs on the bough.

Where the bee sucks nectar, there I suck. I lie in a cowslip's bell, and rest there when owls cry. I fly on a bat's back merrily, following the summer. Merrily, merrily shall I live now, under the blossom that hangs on the branch.

Why, that's my dainty Ariel! I shall miss thee; / But yet thou shalt have freedom;—so, so, so.— / To the king's ship, invisible as thou art: / There shalt thou find the mariners asleep / Under the hatches; the master and the boatswain / Being awake, enforce them to this place, / And presently, I prithee.

That's my dainty Ariel! I'll miss you, but you'll still have your freedom. So, so, so. Go to the King's ship, invisible as you are. There you'll find the sailors asleep below deck. When the captain and the boatswain are awake, make them come here, and at once, please.
I drink the air before me, and return / Or ere your pulse twice beat.
I'll drink the air in front of me and be back before your pulse beats twice.
All torment, trouble, wonder and amazement / Inhabits here. Some heavenly power guide us / Out of this fearful country!
Every torment, trouble, wonder and amazement lives here. May some heavenly power guide us out of this terrifying country!

Behold, sir king, / The wronged Duke of Milan, Prospero. / For more assurance that a living prince / Does now speak to thee, I embrace thy body; / And to thee and thy company I bid / A hearty welcome.
Look, sir King, the wronged Duke of Milan, Prospero. To assure you further that a living prince is speaking to you, I embrace you. And to you and your companions I give a hearty welcome.

Whe'er thou be'st he or no, / Or some enchanted trifle to abuse me, / As late I have been, I not know: thy pulse / Beats, as of flesh and blood; and, since I saw thee, / Th' affliction of my mind amends, with which, / I fear, a madness held me: this must crave,— / An if this be at all—a most strange story. / Thy dukedom I resign, and do entreat / Thou pardon me my wrongs.—But how should Prospero / Be living and be here?

Whether you are him or not, or some enchanted thing to deceive me, as I have been deceived lately, I don't know. Your pulse beats like flesh and blood, and since I saw you, the disorder of my mind, which I'm afraid held me in madness, has got better. This must need, if it is real at all, a very strange story. I give back your dukedom and beg you to pardon my wrongs. But how can Prospero be alive and be here?
First, noble friend, / Let me embrace thine age; whose honour cannot / Be measur'd or confin'd.
First, noble friend, let me embrace you, old man, whose honour cannot be measured or limited.
Whether this be / Or be not, I'll not swear.
Whether this is real or not, I won't swear.

You do yet taste / Some subtleties o' the isle, that will not let you / Believe things certain.—Welcome, my friends all:— / [Aside to SEBASTIAN and ANTONIO] But you, my brace of / lords, were I so minded, / I here could pluck his highness' frown upon you, / And justify you traitors: at this time / I will tell no tales.

You are still feeling some of the island's illusions, which won't let you believe things that are certain. Welcome, all my friends! But you, my pair of lords, if I wanted to, I could bring down his Highness's anger on you right here and prove you traitors. For now I'll tell no tales.
The devil is speaking through him.

No. / For you, most wicked sir, whom to call brother / Would even infect my mouth, I do forgive / Thy rankest fault; all of them; and require / My dukedom of thee, which, perforce, I know / Thou must restore.

No. As for you, most wicked sir, whom it would infect my mouth to call brother, I forgive your foulest crime, all of them, and I demand my dukedom back from you, which I know you have no choice but to return.

If thou beest Prospero, / Give us particulars of thy preservation; / How thou hast met us here, whom three hours since / Were wrack'd upon this shore; where I have lost,— / How sharp the point of this remembrance is!— / My dear son Ferdinand.

If you are Prospero, tell us the details of how you survived, how you've met us here, who were wrecked on this shore three hours ago, where I have lost (how sharply this memory stabs me!) my dear son Ferdinand.
Irreparable is the loss, and patience / Says it is past her cure.
The loss can't be repaired, and patience says it's beyond her power to cure.
I rather think / You have not sought her help; of whose soft grace, / For the like loss I have her sovereign aid, / And rest myself content.
I think rather that you haven't asked for her help. By her gentle mercy I have her powerful aid for a loss just like yours, and I am content.
As great to me, as late; and, supportable / To make the dear loss, have I means much weaker / Than you may call to comfort you, for I / Have lost my daughter.
As great to me, and as recent. And to make such a painful loss bearable I have far weaker comforts than you can call on, because I have lost my daughter.

A daughter? / O heavens! that they were living both in Naples, / The king and queen there! That they were, I wish / Myself were mudded in that oozy bed / Where my son lies. When did you lose your daughter?

A daughter? Oh heavens, if only they were both alive in Naples, as king and queen there! If only they were, I'd wish myself buried in that muddy bed where my son lies. When did you lose your daughter?

In this last tempest. I perceive, these lords / At this encounter do so much admire / That they devour their reason, and scarce think / Their eyes do offices of truth, their words / Are natural breath; but, howsoe'er you have / Been justled from your senses, know for certain / That I am Prospero, and that very duke / Which was thrust forth of Milan; who most strangely / Upon this shore, where you were wrack'd, was landed / To be the lord on't. No more yet of this; / For 'tis a chronicle of day by day, / Not a relation for a breakfast nor / Befitting this first meeting. Welcome, sir: / This cell's my court: here have I few attendants / And subjects none abroad: pray you, look in. / My dukedom since you have given me again, / I will requite you with as good a thing; / At least bring forth a wonder, to content ye / As much as me my dukedom.

In this last storm. I can see that these lords are so amazed at this meeting that they swallow their reason and hardly believe that their eyes are telling the truth or that their words are natural breath. But however much you have been shaken out of your senses, know for certain that I am Prospero, the very duke who was thrown out of Milan, and who, most strangely, landed on this shore where you were wrecked, to be its lord. No more of this yet, because it's a story to be told day by day, not one for over breakfast, nor suitable for this first meeting. Welcome, sir. This cave is my court. Here I have few servants, and no subjects outside. Please, look in. Since you have given me back my dukedom, I'll repay you with something just as good, or at least show you a wonder that will please you as much as my dukedom pleases me.
Sweet lord, you play me false.
No, my dearest love, / I would not for the world.
No, my dearest love, I wouldn't for the world.
Yes, for a score of kingdoms you should wrangle, / And I would call it fair play.
Yes, you would argue over twenty kingdoms, and I would call it fair play.
If this prove / A vision of the island, one dear son / Shall I twice lose.
If this turns out to be another illusion of the island, I'll have lost one dear son twice.
A miracle of the highest kind!
Though the seas threaten, they are merciful: / I have curs'd them without cause. / [Kneels to ALONSO.]
Though the seas threaten, they are merciful. I cursed them without reason.
Now all the blessings / Of a glad father compass thee about! / Arise, and say how thou cam'st here.
Now may all the blessings of a happy father surround you! Stand up and tell me how you came here.
O, wonder! / How many goodly creatures are there here! / How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world / That has such people in't!
Oh, wonder! How many fine creatures there are here! How beautiful mankind is! Oh, splendid new world that has such people in it!
What is this maid, with whom thou wast at play? / Your eld'st acquaintance cannot be three hours: / Is she the goddess that hath sever'd us, / And brought us thus together?
Who is this girl you were playing with? You can't have known her for more than three hours. Is she the goddess who separated us and has brought us together like this?

Sir, she is mortal; / But by immortal Providence she's mine. / I chose her when I could not ask my father / For his advice, nor thought I had one. She / Is daughter to this famous Duke of Milan, / Of whom so often I have heard renown, / But never saw before; of whom I have / Receiv'd a second life: and second father / This lady makes him to me.

Sir, she is mortal, but by immortal Providence she is mine. I chose her when I couldn't ask my father for his advice, and didn't think I had a father. She is the daughter of this famous Duke of Milan, whose fame I have heard of so often but whom I never saw before. From him I have received a second life, and this lady makes him a second father to me.
I am hers: / But, O! how oddly will it sound that I / Must ask my child forgiveness!
And I am a second father to her. But oh, how strange it will sound that I must ask my child to forgive me!
