There, sir, stop: / Let us not burden our remembrances with / A heaviness that's gone.
Stop there, sir. Let's not weigh down our memories with a sadness that's over.
I have inly wept, / Or should have spoke ere this. Look down, you gods, / And on this couple drop a blessed crown; / For it is you that have chalk'd forth the way / Which brought us hither.
I have been weeping inside, or I would have spoken before now. Look down, you gods, and drop a blessed crown on this couple, because it was you who marked out the path that brought us here.

Was Milan thrust from Milan, that his issue / Should become kings of Naples? O, rejoice / Beyond a common joy, and set it down / With gold on lasting pillars. In one voyage / Did Claribel her husband find at Tunis, / And Ferdinand, her brother, found a wife / Where he himself was lost; Prospero his dukedom / In a poor isle; and all of us ourselves, / When no man was his own.

Was the Duke of Milan thrown out of Milan so that his children could become kings of Naples? Oh, rejoice beyond ordinary joy, and write it in gold on lasting pillars! On one voyage Claribel found her husband at Tunis, and Ferdinand, her brother, found a wife where he himself was lost; Prospero found his dukedom on a poor island; and all of us found ourselves, when none of us was in his right mind.
[To FERDINAND and MIRANDA] Give me your hands: / Let grief and sorrow still embrace his heart / That doth not wish you joy!
Give me your hands. May grief and sorrow always grip the heart of anyone who doesn't wish you joy!

O look, sir! look, sir! Here are more of us. / I prophesied, if a gallows were on land, / This fellow could not drown.—Now, blasphemy, / That swear'st grace o'erboard, not an oath on shore? / Hast thou no mouth by land? What is the news?

Oh look, sir! Look, sir! Here are more of us! I predicted that if there was a gallows on land, this fellow couldn't drown. Now, you blasphemer, who swore heaven's grace overboard, not one oath on shore? Have you no mouth on land? What's the news?

The best news is that we have safely found / Our king and company: the next, our ship,— / Which but three glasses since we gave out split,— / Is tight and yare, and bravely rigg'd as when / We first put out to sea.

The best news is that we have found our King and his company safe. The next is that our ship, which only three hours ago we said was wrecked, is watertight, ready and as finely rigged as when we first put out to sea.
[Aside to PROSPERO] Sir, all this service / Have I done since I went.
Sir, I have done all this since I left.
These are not natural events; they strengthen / From strange to stranger—Say, how came you hither?
These are not natural events. They grow stranger and stranger. Tell me, how did you get here?

If I did think, sir, I were well awake, / I'd strive to tell you. We were dead of sleep, / And,—how, we know not,—all clapp'd under hatches, / Where, but even now, with strange and several noises / Of roaring, shrieking, howling, jingling chains, / And mo diversity of sounds, all horrible, / We were awak'd; straightway, at liberty: / Where we, in all her trim, freshly beheld / Our royal, good, and gallant ship; our master / Cap'ring to eye her: on a trice, so please you, / Even in a dream, were we divided from them, / And were brought moping hither.

If I thought I was wide awake, sir, I'd try to tell you. We were fast asleep and, we don't know how, all shut up below deck. Just now we were woken by strange and different noises of roaring, shrieking, howling, jangling chains and more kinds of sounds, all horrible, and at once we were free. There we saw our royal, good and gallant ship in perfect condition, and our captain dancing with joy to see her. In an instant, if you please, as if in a dream, we were separated from the others and brought here in a daze.
[Aside to ARIEL] Bravely, my diligence. Thou / shalt be free.
Splendidly, my busy one. You'll be free.
This is as strange a maze as e'er men trod; / And there is in this business more than nature / Was ever conduct of: some oracle / Must rectify our knowledge.
This is as strange a maze as men ever walked, and there is more in this business than nature ever brought about. Some oracle must explain it to us.

Sir, my liege, / Do not infest your mind with beating on / The strangeness of this business: at pick'd leisure, / Which shall be shortly, single I'll resolve you,— / Which to you shall seem probable—of every / These happen'd accidents; till when, be cheerful / And think of each thing well.—[Aside to ARIEL] Come / hither, spirit; / Set Caliban and his companions free; / Untie the spell. [Exit ARIEL] How fares my gracious sir? / There are yet missing of your company / Some few odd lads that you remember not.

Sir, my lord, don't trouble your mind by hammering on the strangeness of this business. At a chosen time, which will be soon, I'll explain to you in private every one of these events, in a way that will seem believable to you. Until then, be cheerful and think well of everything. Come here, spirit. Set Caliban and his companions free. Undo the spell. How are you, my gracious sir? There are still a few odd fellows of your company missing whom you've forgotten.
Every man shift for all the rest, and let no man / take care for himself, for all is but fortune.—Coragio! / bully-monster, Coragio!
Every man look after all the rest, and let no man care about himself, because everything is just luck. Courage, fine monster, courage!
If these be true spies which I wear in my head, / here's a goodly sight.
If these eyes in my head are telling the truth, here's a fine sight.
O Setebos, these be brave spirits indeed. / How fine my master is! I am afraid / He will chastise me.
Oh Setebos, these are splendid spirits indeed! How fine my master looks! I'm afraid he'll punish me.
Ha, ha! / What things are these, my lord Antonio? / Will money buy them?
Ha, ha! What are these things, my lord Antonio? Can money buy them?
Very like; one of them / Is a plain fish, and, no doubt, marketable.
Very likely. One of them is plainly a fish, and no doubt sellable.

Mark but the badges of these men, my lords, / Then say if they be true.—This mis-shapen knave— / His mother was a witch; and one so strong / That could control the moon, make flows and ebbs, / And deal in her command without her power. / These three have robb'd me; and this demi-devil,— / For he's a bastard one,—had plotted with them / To take my life: two of these fellows you / Must know and own; this thing of darkness I / Acknowledge mine.

Just look at these men's uniforms, my lords, and then say if they're honest. This misshapen rogue's mother was a witch, and such a strong one that she could control the moon, make tides flow and ebb, and use the moon's power without its authority. These three have robbed me, and this half-devil (for he's a bastard one) had plotted with them to take my life. Two of these fellows you must know and claim as yours. This thing of darkness I admit is mine.
I shall be pinch'd to death.
Is not this Stephano, my drunken butler?
Isn't this Stephano, my drunken butler?
He is drunk now: where had he wine?
He's drunk now. Where did he get wine?
And Trinculo is reeling-ripe: where should they / Find this grand liquor that hath gilded them? / How cam'st thou in this pickle?
And Trinculo is staggering drunk. Where did they find this marvellous liquor that has flushed them gold? How did you get into this pickle?
I have been in such a pickle since I saw you / last that, I fear me, will never out of my bones. I / shall not fear fly-blowing.
I've been in such a pickle since I last saw you that I'm afraid it will never get out of my bones. I won't have to worry about flies laying eggs in me.
O! touch me not: I am not Stephano, but a cramp.
Oh, don't touch me! I'm not Stephano, I'm one big cramp.
You'd be king o' the isle, sirrah?
You wanted to be king of the island, did you, fellow?
I should have been a sore one, then.
I'd have been a sore one, then.
This is as strange a thing as e'er I look'd on. / [Pointing to CALIBAN]
This is as strange a thing as I ever looked at.
He is as disproportioned in his manners / As in his shape.—Go, sirrah, to my cell; / Take with you your companions: as you look / To have my pardon, trim it handsomely.
He is as misshapen in his behaviour as in his body. Go to my cave, fellow, and take your companions with you. If you hope for my pardon, tidy it up nicely.
Ay, that I will; and I'll be wise hereafter, / And seek for grace. What a thrice-double ass / Was I, to take this drunkard for a god, / And worship this dull fool!
Yes, I will. And I'll be wise from now on and seek forgiveness. What a triple-double ass I was to take this drunk for a god and worship this stupid fool!
Hence, and bestow your luggage where you found it.
Go, and put that junk back where you found it.

Sir, I invite your Highness and your train / To my poor cell, where you shall take your rest / For this one night; which—part of it—I'll waste / With such discourse as, I not doubt, shall make it / Go quick away; the story of my life / And the particular accidents gone by / Since I came to this isle: and in the morn / I'll bring you to your ship, and so to Naples, / Where I have hope to see the nuptial / Of these our dear-belov'd solemnized; / And thence retire me to my Milan, where / Every third thought shall be my grave.

Sir, I invite your Highness and your followers to my poor cave, where you will rest for this one night. I'll spend part of it with talk that I'm sure will make it pass quickly: the story of my life and all the events that have happened since I came to this island. And in the morning I'll take you to your ship and so to Naples, where I hope to see the wedding of these dearly loved young people celebrated. And from there I'll retire to my Milan, where every third thought will be of my grave.
I long To hear the story of your life, which must / Take the ear strangely.
I long to hear the story of your life, which must be strange to hear.

I'll deliver all; / And promise you calm seas, auspicious gales, / And sail so expeditious that shall catch / Your royal fleet far off.—[Aside to ARIEL] My Ariel, / chick, / That is thy charge: then to the elements / Be free, and fare thou well!—Please you, draw near.

I'll tell you everything, and I promise you calm seas, favourable winds and sailing so fast that you'll catch up with your royal fleet far ahead. My Ariel, my chick, that is your job. Then be free to the elements, and farewell! Please, come in.

Now my charms are all o'erthrown, / And what strength I have's mine own; / Which is most faint; now 'tis true, / I must be here confin'd by you, / Or sent to Naples. Let me not, / Since I have my dukedom got, / And pardon'd the deceiver, dwell / In this bare island by your spell: / But release me from my bands / With the help of your good hands. / Gentle breath of yours my sails / Must fill, or else my project fails, / Which was to please. Now I want / Spirits to enforce, art to enchant; / And my ending is despair, / Unless I be reliev'd by prayer, / Which pierces so that it assaults / Mercy itself, and frees all faults. / As you from crimes would pardon'd be, / Let your indulgence set me free.

Now my spells are all overthrown, and what strength I have is my own, which is very weak. Now it's true that I must either be kept here by you or sent to Naples. Since I have got my dukedom back and pardoned the man who deceived me, don't let me stay on this bare island by your spell, but release me from my bonds with the help of your good hands. Your kind breath must fill my sails, or else my plan fails, which was to please you. Now I have no spirits to command and no magic to enchant, and my ending will be despair unless I am helped by prayer, which pierces so deeply that it storms mercy itself and frees all faults. As you would be pardoned for your sins, let your kindness set me free.
